presentations.presentation_title: Time Scale of Deep-seated Gravitational Slope Deformation in Mountainous Area Composed of Neogene–Quaternary Sedimentary Rock
presentations.abstract: The maximum lifespan of deep-seated gravitational slope deformation (DGSD) is uncertain, but crucial for reconstruction of landscape evolution and disaster prevention. To understand this, field surveys to obtain formation ages are needed. Here, we conducted drilling surveys, tephra analysis and radiocarbon dating to estimate the formation age of DGSD in the Sekita Mountains, central Japan, which are composed of Neogene–Quaternary sedimentary rocks. We targeted three linear depressions: the Nonomi Bog, Chayaike Bog and Kitaburuike Bog from east to west, and obtained NNM-P1, CYI-P1 and KBI-P2 cores, respectively. As a result, nine visible tephras and four cryptotephras in the NNM-P1, four visible tephras and eight cryptotephras in the CYI-P1, and one visible tephra and one cryptotephra in the KBI-P2 were detected. The tephrostratigraphy of NNM-P1 and CYI-P1 has already been reported (Watanabe et al., 2026, Quat. Geochron). This tephrostratigraphy and some radiocarbon dates suggests that formation ages of Nonomi, Chayaike and Kitaburuike bogs are >147 ka, ~42 ka, and ~20 ka, respectively. In addition, fresh scarps around the Chayaike and Kitaburuike bogs indicate that DGSDs around these two bogs are active. In contrast, the Nonomi bog was formed since MIS 6, indicating the second oldest DGSD feature in Japanese archipelago. However, the absence of Holocene sediment in NNM-P1 and the development of gullies on the surface of Nonomi Bog suggest that activity near Nonomi Bog has been dormant in recently. To investigate the reasons for the differences in DGSD activity in the Sekita Mountains, we calculated Coulomb stress changes (ΔCFS) associated with active faulting using Coulomb 3.4 software (Lin and Stein ,2004; Toda et al., 2005). In the presentation, we will discuss the relationship between the activity of DGSD and ΔCFS distribution.

presentations.presentation_title: Satellite-Based Assessment of Slope Instability in Open-Pit Mining Using Multi-Temporal DEMs and InSAR Time-Series Analysis
presentations.institution: Hanoi School of Business and Management, Vietnam National University
presentations.abstract: Open-pit mining is widely used due to its relatively low development costs, but the substantial alteration of terrain often increases the risk of geohazards such as land subsidence and slope failures. While ground-based monitoring systems can provide precise measurements and real-time warnings, their spatial coverage is limited and implementation costs are high. This study presents a satellite-based workflow for assessing slope instability with broad spatial coverage and reduced operational cost. The workflow integrates high-resolution multi-temporal digital elevation models (DEMs) derived from optical imagery to quantify topographic evolution, followed by interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR) time-series analysis to retrieve ground deformation around mining sites. Empirical Mode Decomposition is applied to the InSAR time series to separate non-harmonic seasonal signals from long-term displacement trends. The corrected displacement data are then modeled using a segment-wise linear inverse velocity (INV) approach to estimate temporal changes in time-of-failure, serving as a proxy for slope stability. The workflow is tested at two contrasting sites: Nui Beo coal mine in northern Vietnam, where no slope failure has occurred, and Hpakant jade mine in northern Myanmar, where a catastrophic slope failure in 2020 resulted in over 170 fatalities. The results demonstrate that the proposed workflow effectively captures slope instability and is suitable for operational monitoring and early-warning applications in open-pit mining environments.

presentations.presentation_title: Automatic Calibration of a Random Walk Model for Debris-flow Runout Mapping
presentations.abstract: Estimating debris-flow runout is a key step in hazard assessment. Although physics-based models such as Nays2D are widely used, application of these models often requires extensive input data, including detailed soil properties and field information. The Random Walk Model (RWM) provides a simpler, probabilistic alternative that can simulate debris-flow propagation rapidly with limited inputs. RWM is controlled by four parameters: total released sediment volume (VT), sediment volume per step (VS), gravity weight (IW), and stopping slope (SS). VT can be inferred from pre-/post-event imagery, whereas VS, IW, and SS have typically been tuned manually; manual tuning is time-consuming and may converge to a local optimum. In this study, RWM was coupled with an automatic parameter search to calibrate VS, IW, and SS. The workflow used three datasets: a 5 m resolution DEM, mapped source locations with the observed runout extent, and a binary observation map for objective-function computation. Differential Evolution (DE) was used to search the parameter space, and performance was assessed by pixel-wise agreement between simulated and observed runout maps. DE-based calibration identified an optimal parameter set without manual intervention. The calibrated simulation reproduced 10,884 of 11,801 pixels, achieving 92.23% accuracy for the case study. The results indicate that global optimization can effectively replace manual tuning in RWM while maintaining high agreement with observations. The proposed approach enables fast debris-flow runout mapping when detailed input data are limited.Funding:This work was supported by Korea Environmental Industry&Technology Institute(KEITI) through R&D Program for Innovative Flood Protection Technologies against Climate Crisis Project, funded by Korea Ministry of Environment(MOE)(2022003460002)

presentations.presentation_title: Effects of Wetting–drying Cycles on Slope Erosion and Cracks Evolution Based on Physical Model Experiments and Close-range Photogrammetry
presentations.institution: Department of Civil Engineering, National Pingtung University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Under the influence of climate change, the frequency of alternating extreme rainfall events and high-temperature solar exposure has increased, causing natural slopes to be repeatedly subjected to wetting–drying cycles induced by rainfall and sunlight. These processes intensify surface erosion, crack development, and slope instability. However, most existing studies primarily focus on the effects of single rainfall events on slope deformation and failure, while the cumulative impacts of slope erosion and crack evolution under rainfall–sunlight cyclic conditions remain insufficiently investigated, particularly through high-resolution experimental validation. In this study, a series of laboratory physical model experiments combined with close-range photogrammetry were conducted to investigate the mechanisms governing slope erosion behavior and crack evolution under rainfall–sunlight cycles. Inclined slope models were subjected to two rainfall intensities, 30 mm/hr and 60 mm/hr, and the hydrological and geomorphological responses of the slopes were compared between two scenarios: rainfall-only and rainfall–sunlight cycling conditions. During the experiments, surface runoff, erosion volume, and crack development were monitored. Multi-temporal three-dimensional terrain models were reconstructed using fixed-position image acquisition, enabling millimeter-scale quantification of topographic changes and erosion volumes. The results indicate that slopes subjected to rainfall–sunlight cycles exhibit more pronounced topographic degradation and structural damage than those under rainfall-only conditions. Soil shrinkage and crack formation induced during the drying phase create preferential infiltration pathways during subsequent rainfall events. Cracks developed near the slope crest promote erosion and progressive failure, leading to an increase in erosion volume, particularly under high rainfall intensity conditions (60 mm/hr). In addition, the increased density and spatial complexity of crack networks alter surface runoff pathways, accelerating microtopographic evolution and surface material loss. Furthermore, the integration of close-range photogrammetry with physical model experiments effectively captures the spatiotemporal evolution of slope erosion and crack development under wetting–drying cycles.

presentations.presentation_title: Assessment of the Impact of Weather Extremes on Landslides in the Darjeeling Himalayan Region
presentations.abstract: The Darjeeling Himalayan region has experienced recurring disasters throughout recorded history. Major landslides occurred in 1899, 1934, 1950, 1968, 1975, 1980, 1991, 2011, and 2015. In 1968, continuous rainfall of 1,000 mm over 52 hours triggered numerous landslides, resulting in casualties exceeding one thousand. Intense rainfall during 4–5 October 2025 triggered about 500 landslides of varying types and magnitudes across the Darjeeling Himalayan region. Landslides have been identified using SoI toposheets at 1:50,000 and satellite imagery. The distribution of landslides indicates that the number of new landslides exceeds the number of old slides. The present research includes an analysis of rainfall data and secondary sources on landslides to examine the occurrence of continuous landslide incidents throughout the rainy season in the Darjeeling Himalayan region. Several statistical indicators are used to demonstrate the variability of rainfall during this period. A pattern has emerged, with failures occurring in October during 1968, 2015, and 2025, suggesting possible shifts in regional climatic conditions. There is an increase in the occurrence of high-intensity rainfall events during the post-monsoon period. The resulting landslides outside the traditional monsoon season potentially indicate an extension of the period when slopes are vulnerable to hydrological stress.

presentations.presentation_title: Simulating Long-term Coastal Dune Evolution with Sand Fence Implementation
presentations.abstract: Coastal dunes play an important role as natural buffers for coastal protection. However, rising sea levels and associated changes in sediment availability have led to the loss of beaches and coastal dunes. Among the interventions used to enhance dune development, sand fences have been widely applied as a green infrastructure management measure. Understanding how sand fences influence dune evolution is therefore essential. This research aims to reproduce coastal dune evolution under combined wave, wind, and sea level changes, building on the semi-empirical beach profile model, the (Cross-Shore) CS model. While the CS model represents sediment transport across the bar, berm, and dune, it does not account for the alteration of wind shear velocity caused by the sand fences. Accordingly, the sand fence effect will be considered in the aeolian transport calculation for the model development. Using data from Hasaki Beach, this study focuses on the period from 1991 to 2006, during which the local government periodically installed the sand fences. The model development attempts to reproduce the observed initial vertical growth, followed by the seaward horizontal growth of the dune. Validation was conducted using both observed beach profiles and Structure-from-Motion (SfM)–derived elevation data from historical aerial photographs. Including the sand fence effect contributes to a better understanding of dune evolution mechanisms and demonstrates the potential of integrating sand fences as an effective green infrastructure strategy for coastal dune management.

presentations.presentation_title: Rainfall Thresholds for Landslide-induced Sediment Processes by Landslide Type
presentations.abstract: Rainfall thresholds are primary tools for issuing landslide early warnings to minimize impacts. Rainfall event characteristics strongly influence the resulting landslide types. However, studies addressing variations in rainfall thresholds among different landslide types remain limited, resulting in substantial knowledge gaps. Therefore, this study characterizes the effects of landslide type on rainfall thresholds using rainfall data and data on three landslide types (slope failures, SF; debris flows, DF; and deep-seated rapid landslides, DSLS), mainly from the Kii Peninsula, Japan. Hourly rainfall data were collected from 71 rainfall stations during 2009–2018, including rainfall events in 1982 and 2004 that triggered DSLS. From these records, 17,905 rainfall events were separated, and cumulative event rainfall, E (mm), and rainfall event duration, D (h), were calculated. Data for 411 SF, 78 DF, and 77 DSLS were compiled. Among all rainfall events, 260 (1.5%), 42 (0.2%), and 22 (0.1%) events triggered SF, DF, and DSLS, respectively, indicating that rainfall events associated with SF occurred approximately 8 and 15 times more frequently than those associated with DF and DSLS.For landslide triggering, E was plotted against D, and minimum power-law E–D thresholds were fitted separately for each landslide type. The derived thresholds are E = 3.137 × D 0.5265 (7 ≤ D ≤ 242 h), E = 4.007 × D 0.7514 (19 ≤ D ≤ 144 h), and E = 5.463 × D 0.9518 (66 ≤ D ≤ 139 h) for SF, DF, and DSLS, respectively. For durations of 12–144 h, threshold E amounts for triggering DF and DSLS were approximately 2–4 times and 5–14 times higher than those for SF. Differences in triggering mechanisms among landslide types likely explain these variations. These results highlight the importance of defining rainfall thresholds according to landslide type to improve landslide early warning accuracy.

presentations.presentation_title: Controls of Geology and Topography on Landslide Size and Mobility
presentations.abstract: Understanding controls on landslide size and mobility is essential for improving hazard assessment and runout prediction. This study investigates landslide geometric characteristics and mobility using detailed inventories from four sites in Japan and three in Sri Lanka, spanning sedimentary, igneous, and metamorphic lithologies. Initiation metrics (area Aᵢ, length Lᵢ), total dimensions (area Aₜ, length Lₜ), and normalized mobility indices (Aₜ/Aᵢ, Lₜ/Lᵢ) were analyzed in relation to slope length and relief. Size–frequency analyses reveal distinct regional patterns. Mean rollover areas range from 320–370 m² in some Japanese sites of Uchikawa, Hiroshima, and Asakura to 530–700 m² in Ikawa and Sri Lanka. Power-law exponents (α) vary from 2.3–2.9 (Japan) to 1.8–2.0 (Sri Lanka), indicating heavier tails and greater contribution of large landslides in Sri Lanka. Strong scaling relationships emerge between initiation and total dimensions. Total area (Aₜ) scales nearly linearly with initiation area (Aᵢ) in log–log space, with slopes of 0.95–1.07 and R² = 0.68–0.86. Total length (Lₜ) scales with initiation length (Lᵢ) with slopes of 1.06–1.26 and R² = 0.58–0.84, demonstrating that initiation geometry controls final dimensions. Steeper Lₜ–Lᵢ slopes reflect systematic downslope elongation, particularly pronounced in Hiroshima. Despite consistent geometric scaling, mobility indices show clear regional contrasts. Sri Lankan metamorphic terrains display systematically higher Aₜ/Aᵢ and Lₜ/Lᵢ ratios and greater variability than Japanese sites, reflecting differences in weathering profiles, material strength, and hillslope morphology.. While initiation size determines event scale, post-initiation propagation is strongly controlled by topography and material properties. The findings demonstrate that landslide size and mobility emerge from coupled controls: initiation conditions set baseline scale, while topographic relief and material properties govern runout extent. This framework provides a quantitative basis for improving regional runout prediction and hazard assessment across diverse environments.

presentations.presentation_title: Long-term Evaluation of Grain-size-specific Discharge-sediment Hysteresis Using Riverbed Deformation Analysis: a Case Study of the Lower Abukuma River, Japan
presentations.abstract: Discharge–sediment hysteresis is a fundamental characteristic of suspended sediment transport during flood events and has been widely applied to diagnose sediment sources and transport processes. Hysteresis patterns are commonly interpreted using the Hysteresis Index (HI), yet most applications treat suspended sediment as a bulk quantity, lumping together all grain-size fractions. The hysteresis behaviour of sand-sized sediments, which contribute to the morphology of rivers and coasts, is not sufficiently understood. We evaluated grain-size-specific hysteresis using a long-term riverbed deformation model over a 20-year period (2000–2019). The analysis focused on an approximately 37-km reach that extended upstream from the river mouth across the low-gradient alluvial plain of the Abukuma River, Japan. Hysteresis patterns were analysed for three major flood events in 2002, 2011, and 2019, with emphasis on their spatial and temporal variability. The results show clear spatial contrasts in the hysteresis behaviour between grain-size classes. Very fine sand exhibited consistent anticlockwise hysteresis throughout the reach, indicating transport dominated by upstream supply with minimal riverbed interaction. Fine sand showed spatially variable hysteresis, shifting from anticlockwise upstream to clockwise near the river mouth, where flood-induced erosion of the riverbed reduced its proportion of bed-material. Medium sand, coarse sand, and very coarse sand showed alternating hysteresis patterns along the reaches, corresponding to spatially heterogeneous zones of erosion and deposition. These findings demonstrate that the hysteresis patterns reflect the relative dominance of the entrainment of bed-material versus the supply of upstream sediments. Clockwise hysteresis emerges where local erosion enhances suspended sediment flux during rising discharge, while anticlockwise hysteresis indicates delayed suspended sediment transport controlled by upstream inputs. Balanced conditions are likely to result in weak or complex hysteresis patterns. This framework provides a physically based interpretation of grain-size-dependent hysteresis and offers new insights into sediment dynamics in lowland rivers.

presentations.presentation_title: The Effects of Dam-induced Vegetation Encroachment and Channel Separation Between Thalweg and Bars on Effective Discharge
presentations.abstract: Bankfull discharge is used in regime equations because it closely matches effective discharge, which contributes most to sediment transport. Effective discharge is defined as the discharge at which the product of sediment transport rate and flow frequency is maximized. In recent years, channels with clear separation between thalweg and depositional areas, accompanied by vegetation encroachment, have increased. However, the effect of this separation on effective discharge is not well understood. In this study, we investigate the impact of this separation on effective discharge using two-dimensional bed variation analysis for the Chubetsu River in Hokkaido.We analyzed eight cross-sections from 12.6 km to 22.6 km downstream of the river mouth during two periods: 1975 before dam construction and 2012 after construction. After dam construction, channel branching and vegetation expansion progressed. Due to limited observed flow records, we estimated flow frequency using d4PDF rainfall data for dam presence and absence under current climate conditions. We applied the Nays2DH model using cross-sectional topography, riverbed sediment, and vegetation data. We calculated effective discharge () from the relationship between discharge, sediment transport, and discharge frequency. We estimated bankfull discharge () from the head-flow (H-Q) curve obtained from simulations and compared the dimensionless river width () with the observed value ().As a result, effective discharge decreased after the separation. Vegetation growth and bed coarsening suppressed sediment transport, while channel narrowing enhanced sediment transport at low discharges. In addition, dam operation increased discharges below 200 m³/s, which raised the contribution of medium flows to sediment transport. These combined effects have likely led to the decrease in effective discharge. Furthermore, a larger was associated with a larger , indicating insufficient sediment transport at bankfull discharge where channel width exceeds the stable width.

presentations.presentation_title: Changes in Mixed-grain Sediment Transport Rate with Alluvial Cover Ratio in a Mixed Bedrock-alluvial Channel
presentations.abstract: In the transport of mixed-grain sediments, smaller sediments are more difficult to mobilize due to the hiding effect of larger sediments. In bedrock rivers with complex irregularities, this phenomenon is expected to be more pronounced because of the additional hiding effect induced by bedrock roughness. However, the existing models for mixed grain-size sediment transport have been developed and applied primarily to alluvial beds, and their applicability to mixed alluvial-bedrock beds has not been confirmed. In this study, we investigate the transport rates of mixed-size sediments over a rough bedrock bed and compare the results with existing models.We used an experimental channel that simulated the bedrock surface by embedding 30 mm gravels. We supplied mixed-grain sediments that are composed of four particle sizes (0.77 mm, 1.42 mm, 2.84 mm, 5 mm) with a mixing ratio of 1:1:1:1. A total of 20 experimental runs were conducted, combining four different flow discharges with five different sediment supply rates. The relationship between the alluvial cover 6-8-44ratio and the sediment transport rate was analyzed for each grain size. Moreover, we introduced correction factors into the existing models and determined these factors to match the experimental results.The results show that when the bed was completely alluvial, the existing models and the experimental results generally agreed. However, as sediment supply decreased and the bed became a mixed bedrock-alluvial bed, the existing models overestimated the experimental results. The correction factor that determines from the existing models depended on the ratio of the alluvial thickness to the bedrock roughness height (η/L). This suggests that η/L should be incorporated into bedload models to account for the hiding effect on a mixed bedrock-alluvial channel.

presentations.presentation_title: Sediment Production and Runoff in the Mountainous Upstream of the Tadami River, Japan
presentations.abstract: In the Tadami River, flowing through the Aizu region of Fukushima Prefecture, sediment production has become increasingly active since the Niigata-Fukushima Heavy Rain in 2011. This trend is particularly significant in the tributaries and mountainous headwaters. Consequently, sedimentation has progressed remarkably in the series of cascading hydroelectric dams within the basin, making countermeasures an urgent priority. Since the Aizu region is characterized by heavy winter snowfall, sediment transport is expected to be substantial not only during summer floods but also during the spring snowmelt season. Therefore, an accurate understanding of the sediment load and the timing of its increase is essential for effective dam management. This study analyzed recent sediment runoff data in the upper Tadami River basin and compared it across different seasons to examine the characteristics of transport during the snowmelt period and identify challenges for sedimentation mitigation.

presentations.presentation_title: Physically-based Macro-scale Formulation of Sediment Transport
presentations.abstract: Predicting continental-scale riverline sediment dynamics remains a persistent challenge in hydrology and earth sciences. While micro-scale models accurately capture local processes, directly applying their governing equations to macro-scale grids often leads to numerical instabilities and a loss of physical clarity. Consequently, researchers have frequently resorted to empirical or lumped models for global applications, sacrificing the physical explainability required to understand the mechanistic drivers of riverbed aggradation and degradation. Moreover, these empirical approaches are inherently limited by historical observation ranges, making them less reliable for predicting responses to unprecedented extreme events. This study advances CaMa-SED, a sediment transport framework integrated into the global river routing model CaMa-Flood, by replacing local-dependent mechanics with macro-scale-consistent physical representations to enhance both explainability and stability. We introduce two strategic enhancements to improve the model's physical explainability and scalability: (1) Stream power-based transport capacity, which utilizes discharge and slope as fundamental energy variables to provide a more scalable representation of sediment dynamics than traditional shear stress-based equations; and (2) an equilibrium concentration scheme using exponential relaxation, which significantly enhances numerical stability and eliminates the time-step dependency and oscillations observed in the original CaMa-SED. Results from the Missouri River basin demonstrate that this scheme achieves high stability in sediment flux and concentration across a wide range of time steps. Current ongoing work focuses on the integration of riverbed evolution feedback. To overcome the numerical challenges of channel aggradation and degradation in macro-scale grids, we are implementing the sediment transportation in the floodplain. This framework aims to overcome the over/underestimation of suspended sediment flux caused by binary river-floodplain partitioning in macro-scale models. By establishing a physically-explainable foundation, this model enables the stable, multi-decadal simulations of "source-to-sink" sediment movement, providing for understanding how continental-scale river morphology responds to environmental shifts and human interventions.

presentations.presentation_title: Long-term Geomorphic and Sediment Budget Responses to Sediment Replenishment Under Dam-regulated Flood Regimes in the Naka River, Japan
presentations.institution: Water Resources Research Center, Disaster Prevention Research Institute (DPRI), Kyoto University
presentations.abstract: This study examines long-term geomorphic responses and sediment budget evolution under the combined influences of sediment replenishment (SR), dam operation, and flood dynamics in the Naka River, Japan. By integrating threshold-based flood frequency analysis, multitemporal geomorphic change detection, and sediment grain-size characterization, we assess the spatial extent and effectiveness of SR over a decadal timescale. Geomorphically effective floods were identified using a Peaks-Over-Threshold (POT) analysis of long-term discharge records. An optimal threshold of 357.55 m³/s delineated flows capable of inducing significant morphological change and successfully captured major typhoon events, including the extreme 2014 flood (5,411 m³/s; 134-year return period). Bathymetric DEMs from 2010–2015 were analyzed using the Difference of DEM (DoD) techniques to quantify erosion and deposition. Results indicate pronounced incision at the SR site (up to −0.89 m) and downstream aggradation reaching +0.65 m within the meandering mid-reach (7–14 km), providing clear evidence of downstream dispersal of replenished sediment. Sediment budget analysis reveals peak geomorphic adjustment during 2013–2014 in response to high-magnitude typhoon floods. Subsequent stabilization of sediment volumes suggests partial system recovery and redistribution of SR material, with deposition dominating overall from 2010 to 2015. Cross-sectional analyses confirm active lateral migration associated with bend-scale erosion and deposition, whereas reaches beyond 14 km exhibited limited change due to backwater effects from the Kawaguchi Dam. Grain-size analyses (2014–2025) show poorly sorted, multimodal sediments at the SR site and progressive downstream fining and improved sorting. Field surveys in 2025 identified newly formed bars with grain-size characteristics closely match SR material, indicating sediment transport within one year. Collectively, these results demonstrate that SR effectiveness is strongly controlled by flood magnitude, channel planform, and downstream hydraulic constraints, highlighting the importance of integrated hydrological and geomorphic assessment for sustainable sediment management in dam-regulated rivers.

presentations.presentation_title: Dynamic Equilibrium of Soil Thickness from Ridges to Planar Hillslopes: Field Evaluation Using 10Be-Constrained Nonlinear, Slope-Dependent Soil Transport Model
presentations.abstract: Understanding hillslope evolution and soil development requires evaluating the dynamic equilibrium of soil thickness using soil transport laws applicable across a wide range of slope gradients. On gentle convex ridge crests, soil thickness is maintained in dynamic equilibrium through a balance between soil production from bedrock weathering and soil transport, which increases linearly with gradient. Previous numerical models have shown that steeper slopes extending downslope from ridges require nonlinear, slope-dependent soil transport. However, few field studies have tested whether the model can explain steady-state soil thickness across eroding hillslopes. This study evaluates dynamic equilibrium on granodiorite hillslopes in the northern Abukuma Mountains, Japan. Parameters of the nonlinear, slope-dependent soil transport model and soil production function were constrained using meteoric and in situ 10 Be. Soil production rates were estimated from in situ 10 Be at the base of soils on hill-noses. Soil transport parameters were derived by estimating soil creep fluxes from meteoric 10 Be along a continuous hillslope transect spanning ridge tops, planar midsections, and slightly concave, infilling valley-head hollows. The mass conservation equation under steady state provided theoretical relationships among soil thickness, slope gradient, and curvature, which were compared with DEM-derived curvature. Model predictions support dynamic equilibrium from ridge crests to planar midsections, except in valley-head hollows. The theoretical curvature slightly overestimates the measured values on the hillslope transect with directly estimated soil creep fluxes, but these deviations are systematic and within method uncertainty. Good agreement was also observed on surrounding eroding slopes. Some anomalies likely reflect short-term disturbances, such as recent typhoon-driven heavy rainfall, while overestimation at valley heads implies ongoing soil accumulation. These results demonstrate that combining 10 Be-constrained soil production functions with nonlinear, slope-dependent soil transport enables field-based evaluation of dynamic equilibrium. This approach further provides a process-based geomorphic framework for identifying departures from equilibrium that may precede landslides.

presentations.presentation_title: Representing Secondary Forests, Forest Age Structure, and Management-driven Harvest Dynamics in the Global Vegetation Model Visit
presentations.abstract: Forest management associated with afforestation, wood harvest, and forest regrowth has become an increasingly important anthropogenic driver of the terrestrial carbon cycle. However, most dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs) represent forest management impacts using average biomass density approaches, which limits their ability to capture forest age dynamics and management-driven carbon fluxes.Here we present a set of model developments in the global vegetation model VISIT aimed at improving the representation of secondary forests and forest management processes. First, secondary forests were introduced as an independent vegetation type, with key physiological parameters—including specific leaf area, maximum photosynthesis rate, and leaf litterfall rate—updated based on field observations to better reflect their ecological characteristics. Second, forests were classified into six age classes, and steady-state biomass thresholds for each age class were derived from spin-up simulations under fixed climate and land-use conditions. Third, these biomass thresholds were applied in transient simulations to regulate harvesting, clearing, and regrowth processes, with harvesting and clearing processes regulated by age-dependent biomass thresholds, preferentially targeting older age classes, and with distinct mature-stand and young-stand removal rules applied separately to primary and secondary forests.Idealized transient simulations demonstrate that the improved framework can realistically represent forest age transitions and carbon source–sink dynamics under land-use change and management scenarios. Compared with the original model configuration, the age-structured management scheme leads to more realistic carbon flux responses under land-use change and forest management scenarios.Our developments provide a practical approach for incorporating anthropogenic forest management and forest demographic processes into Earth system models, with implications for improving historical carbon budget assessments and future terrestrial carbon sink projections.

presentations.presentation_title: Records of Human Intervention in Rapidly-developing Pingtan Island, China
presentations.institution: State Key Laboratory of Submarine Geoscience, School of Oceanography, Shanghai Jiao Tong University
presentations.abstract: Ground penetrating radar (GPR) has advanced our understanding of how “natural” coastal systems evolve. A less studied aspect centers on the effects of human impacts to coastal beach-dune systems, specifically artificial dune construction, sand fences, sand mining, artificial planting, and beach nourishment. The coastline of Pingtan Island, Fujian Province, China is an exceptional case study exhibiting various stages of engineering projects that aim to promote tourism and the local economy. The island’s coastline is experiencing severe erosion caused in part by strong NE prevailing winds and typhoons leaving coastal managers with a daunting task of balancing coastal protection with local interests and economic growth. This study focuses on five representative beaches along the entire island integrating multi-frequency GPR surveys, grain size analysis, and online interviews. Two beaches, Changjiang'ao and Tannan Bay represent modified and “natural” endmembers, respectively. Grain size analysis and GPR surveys suggest that engineering activities in Changjiang'ao have accelerated coastal retreat, whereas; Tannan Bay exhibits a more resilient beach-dune system. An extreme case of severe erosion is found in Da'ao, where a combination of sand mining, animal grazing, and vegetation loss has resulted in an eroding dune system. Radargrams from these three beaches show evidence of transgressing dunes, whereas Yufan beach and Shanqi'ao are nourished beaches lacking a well-defined dune system, relatively uniform grain size and parallel/hyperbolic reflectors that are not typical of natural beach-dune systems. Local and tourist perceptions also confirm that the majority of engineering activities (i.e., vegetation planting, facility construction, and bulldozing/beach grading) occur in Changjiang'ao, which is the most visited beach on the island. Collectively, these findings aim to better inform management strategies for sustainably balancing tourism and coastal protection. Our ultimate goal is to raise awareness of how people are affecting the coastline of Pingtan Island and why this is important.

presentations.presentation_title: Reshaping Estuarine Dynamics: Morphological Alterations and Their Implications on Estuarine Salinification in the Vietnamese Mekong Delta
presentations.abstract: Estuarine salinification is a fundamental process that plays a crucial role in shaping estuarine dynamics. However, the long-term interplay between salinity regimes and morphological alterations across the entire Vietnamese Mekong Delta (VMD) remains insufficiently investigated. This study integrated salinity concentration trends to clarify how estuarine salinification evolved in concert with riverbed incision and riverbank migration. Long-term daily maximum salinity measurements (1998 - 2020) were examined using nonparametric statistical tests: the Mann-Kendall test to detect monotonic trends, Sen’s slope to quantify rates of change, and the Pettitt test to identify abrupt shifts. Additionally, bathymetric datasets from 1998, 2005, 2017, and 2020, coupled with remote sensing-based assessment of riverbank erosion over the same time span, were utilized to scrutinize the interrelation between estuarine salinification and morphological changes in the VMD. Across the VMD, the Sen’s slope values at both estuary mouths and upstream stations recorded average rates of 1 PSU/year, mirroring the pronounced morphological transformations of riverbeds and banks, especially during 2017-2020. Moreover, in Dinh An estuary, salinity escalation remained confined to the mouth, reflecting localized tidal reconfiguration while maintaining a stable salt wedge circulation regime. Conversely, Co Chien exhibited elevated salinity trends at both the mouth and 30 km upstream, indicating intensified inland salinity propagation driven by channel deepening and alerting mixing conditions. Although both estuaries share the same marine boundary, their differing responses underscore that internal morphological influences primarily govern estuarine salinity patterns. Overall, these findings reveal how morphological evolution directly reshapes estuarine dynamics, posing significant risks to agro-aquaculture productivity, freshwater availability, and the long-term resilience of deltaic livelihoods.

presentations.presentation_title: Eco-morphodynamic modeling of an active meandering sandy river
presentations.institution: Korea Institute of Civil Engineering and Building Technology
presentations.abstract: Many of the Korean rivers have recently undergone a transformation in their landscape. A key factor is the development of vegetation, transforming bare streams composed of exposed depositional bars into lush ones characterized by dense riparian vegetation. This transformation reflects not only anthropogenic alterations but also broader climatic influences. As climate change progresses, it is expected to further reshape fluvial landscapes by altering hydrological regimes and driving changes in the timing and extent of riparian vegetation. Variations in rainfall and temperature, in particular, directly influence seed disperal, germination timing, growth rates of seedlings, and vegetation mortality, thereby affecting fluvial morphology through complex biogeomorphic feedbacks.This study improves upon an existing eco-morphodynamic model by incorporating the effects of precipitation and temperature on key stages of the riparian vegetation life cycle—germination, growth, and mortality. The revised model introduces logic to reset accumulated dry days based on rainfall events and triggers germination when precipitation exceeds a pre-defined threshold during the germination period. Additionally, temperature-based mechanisms allow early germination if thermal requirements are satisfied ahead of schedule. Growth dynamics are adjusted by modifying the growth curve in response to temperature conditions during germination and development phases. When both rainfall and temperature conditions are met, temperature is prioritized as the primary germination trigger.A comparison of the revised model with its earlier version demonstrates the critical role of climatic variables in realistic simulations of interplay between riparian vegetation and fluvial processes. These improvements enable the model to better capture potential shifts in vegetation phenology and spatial distribution under changing climate conditions. Ultimately, the results provide insight into how fluvial and riparian ecological processes may co-evolve in response to climate variability, supporting more integrated approaches to river management and ecological restoration.

presentations.presentation_title: MTInSAR for Small-scale and Under Canopy Landslides Monitoring
presentations.abstract: Abstract The intensification of extreme rainfall has exacerbated widespread landslide hazards, particularly in tropic and subtropic regions. Hong Kong—the world’s most densely populated city situated on steep, forested terrain—faces chronic landslide risks that are challenging to monitor with conventional Aperture Radar Interferometry (InSAR), as hillslope motions are typically small and hidden beneath dense canopy. In this presentation, we introduce a novel detection framework integrating: 1) HARMIE (Homogeneous Amplitude-phase RefineMent for local Inconsistent phase Estimation), which enhances localized phase variability for subtle displacement retention; and 2) a phase gradient-based detection approach, linking slope responses with extreme rainfall. Using high-resolution ascending and descending Lutan-1 (LT-1) SAR datasets (July 2023–October 2024) over Lantau Island, Hong Kong, the framework mapped widespread hillslope failures triggered by the October 2023 extreme rainfalls, with notable improvements in capturing subtle failures as narrow as ~10 m. Ten active landslides concealed beneath forests were also pinpointed. Beyond detection, our analysis reveals that prolonged antecedent rainfall drives seasonal progressive creep on minor slopes and, for certain slopes, may interact with extreme rainfall to accelerate destabilization. This study maps small, forest-covered landslides in Hong Kong and offers new insights into advancing the development of landslide early-warning systems in such regions.

presentations.presentation_title: From Parameter Interpretation to Hazard Screening: a Transferable Large Woody Debris Export Framework for Data-limited Catchments
presentations.abstract: Large woody debris (LWD) export during extreme rainfall can intensify flooding by clogging channels and infrastructure, yet LWD records are scarce outside monitored dam basins. We present a framework that links a physically motivated LWD exportmodel to measurable watershed properties and rainfall return levels for practical hazard screening. We apply the LWD export model to 11 Japanese dam watersheds using annual LWD export observations from 1996–2021. Model parameters are estimated using a Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) criterion, NSE ranges from 0.483 to 0.995, indicating good reproduction of the largest export years and variable performance for smaller events. To interpret parameter variability, we compile watershed descriptors (area, slope, forest cover, and rainfall indices) and test parameter–property relationships. Several descriptors show strong correlations, notably the area of forested slopes steeper than 20° (r = 0.83) and 3-year return precipitation (r = 0.65), but linear regression generalization remains limited (best in-sample R² ≈ 0.55 with weak cross-validation), suggesting that broader samples and refined predictors are needed. We further develop a hazard assessment approach that couples’ rainfall frequency analysis (24-h extremes) with simulated LWD export volumes (minimum/expected/maximum) under respective initial storage states. Validation against the 1996–2021 record demonstrates feasibility for dam-scale screening and preparedness planning and outlines a path toward transferring LWD hazard assessment to data-limited catchments.

presentations.presentation_title: Enhancing Landslide Early Warning Through Participatory Monitoring: a Community-engaged Approach in Mountainous Region, Nepal
presentations.institution: National Society for Earthquake Technology - Nepal
presentations.abstract: Landslides pose a significant threat to Nepal’s mountainous and hilly landscapes, impacting lives, infrastructure, and livelihoods. Traditional landslide monitoring systems often rely on centralized, technology-intensive models that may be costly, limited in spatial coverage, and disconnected from local knowledge. This study investigates the effectiveness of participatory landslide monitoring as a complementary approach that integrates community engagement, local observations, and low-cost sensing techniques to improve landslide awareness and early warning capacities. Drawing on a mixed-methods research design, we partnered with vulnerable communities in Bhotekoshi area to co-develop a monitoring framework that blends indigenous hazard knowledge, systematic field observations, and simple geotechnical indicators (e.g., surface cracks, soil moisture, ground vibration). Community volunteers were trained to use mobile data collection tools and reporting protocols to record hazard signs and trigger alerts. These locally generated data were integrated with remote sensing products and rainfall measurements to refine hazard assessments and validate community observations. Preliminary results demonstrate that participatory monitoring fosters heightened risk perception, strengthens social networks for disaster preparedness, and generates high-resolution, site-specific data that are often missed by conventional monitoring systems. Communities reported improved confidence in recognizing early warning signs and increased coordination with local authorities in landslide response planning.The study concludes that participatory landslide monitoring is a viable and scalable strategy for enhancing community resilience, especially in resource-limited settings. It underscores the importance of fostering bidirectional knowledge exchange between scientific institutions and local stakeholders and proposes recommendations for policy frameworks that institutionalize community roles in multi-hazard monitoring networks.

presentations.presentation_title: Spatiotemporal Characterization of Pore Pressure Transients in Dip-slope Rock Masses: an Integrated Approach Using Fiber-optic Sensing, Fully Grouted Piezometers and Multi-level Water-level Monitoring
presentations.abstract: The stability of dip slopes in fractured rock masses is critically governed by the transient behavior of groundwater and the resulting pore water pressure distribution along discontinuities. Traditional observation wells often provide a depth-averaged hydraulic head, which fails to capture the high-gradient pressure changes occurring at specific bedding planes or shear zones. This study utilizes a unique experimental site at the Yangming Campus of NYCU university, situated on a rock dip slope, to investigate the complex interactions between groundwater flow, rock permeability, and slope stability. The research integrates data from a specialized 9-borehole monitoring network featuring diverse sensing technologies. This includes traditional dual-layered observation wells (AH1-1, AH2-1, AH3-1), advanced Fiber-Optic Sensing (FOS) for pressure monitoring (AH1-2, AH3-2), and a multi-level system (AH4-2) featuring 18 isolated zones at 2-meter intervals. Rock core samples obtained from four boreholes (AH1-1, AH2-1, AH3-1, AH4-1) are subjected to laboratory testing to determine secondary porosity, hydraulic conductivity, and shear strength parameters of the rock mass and discontinuities.The primary objective is to characterize the three-dimensional groundwater flow field and its response to episodic rainfall events. By comparing the high-resolution data from the 18-layer AH4-2 well with the fiber-optic data, the study aims to quantify the vertical hydraulic connectivity between different lithological units. The integration of these water level monitoring methods allows for the development of a more accurate hydro-geological model for dip slopes. The findings are expected to reveal how transient localized pressures—often missed by conventional monitoring—trigger slope deformations.

presentations.presentation_title: Integrating Spatial Data and Artificial Intelligence (ai) in Forecasting Landslides in Mountainous Regions of Vietnam
presentations.abstract: Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards in mountainous regions, posing serious threats to human life, infrastructure, and ecosystems. Their occurrence is influenced by a combination of natural factors, such as intense rainfall, steep terrain, geological structures, soil properties, and groundwater conditions, as well as human activities including deforestation, road construction, and unsustainable land-use practices. Due to their complex triggering mechanisms and rapid development, landslides remain difficult to predict accurately.This study applies an integrated landslide forecasting and hazard assessment approach using satellite remote sensing, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Multi-Criteria Analysis (MCA), and artificial intelligence (AI) techniques to identify landslide-prone areas in mountainous regions of Vietnam. Multiple conditioning and triggering factors are incorporated, including Digital Elevation Model (DEM)-derived slope and elevation, land use and land cover extracted from Sentinel-2 imagery using supervised classification and the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), soil and geological fault maps, road networks, and observed and forecasted rainfall data obtained from satellite sources and real-time APIs. Each factor is standardized and weighted according to its relative contribution to landslide susceptibility, and GIS-based spatial analysis is applied to generate landslide susceptibility and hazard maps classified into very high, high, moderate, and low hazard levels.After validating the model, the resulting datasets are used to train an AI-based predictive model for forecasting potential landslide occurrences in future periods. The results demonstrate that the integration of spatial data, satellite-derived rainfall information, GIS, MCA, and AI techniques enables near real-time landslide hazard prediction with improved accuracy. This approach provides valuable support for landslide early warning systems, disaster risk reduction, and sustainable land use management in landslide-prone mountainous areas in Vietnam.

presentations.presentation_title: Effects of Particle Size and Mixing Ratio on Soil Bed Erosion and Transport in Collisional Granular Flows
presentations.abstract: Debris flows occurring at the top of a mountain can increase in volume by entraining sediments along the valley and eroding the basal bed. In particular, the debris flow was characterized by the presence of numerous boulders and coarse particles, and it has been reported that the front part of debris flows containing such materials causes substantial erosion due to high collisional stresses are generated. Moreover, bed erosion, the process by which the bed material fails under loadings of debris flow, is one of the most critical factors governing the destructive power of debris flows. In this study, a small-scale flume was made to simulate collisional granular flow and erodible bed, and then the experiments were performed by varying particle size and mixing ratio of glass beads. High-speed cameras were installed on the sides and top of the flume to record the erosion and transport behavior of the granular flow and eroded bed. After the experiment, the effects of particle size and mixing ratio on the erosion and transport of the eroded bed were compared and analyzed. The results indicated that the presence of boulders intensified the interaction between the particles and the basal bed, leading to an increase in sediment transport. Moreover, as the proportion of boulder increased, the amount of sediment transport increased.

presentations.presentation_title: Interpretable Inundation Forecasting: a Shap-based Analysis of Feature Importance and Comparative Selection Methodology
presentations.abstract: Accurate and timely inundation forecasting is a cornerstone of effective disaster mitigation and urban resilience, particularly in regions prone to intense pluvial flooding. This study employs the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method to systematically quantify and rank the importance of various input features for inundation forecasting. Furthermore, the SHAP-based feature attributions are compared with feature selection outcomes from previous literature to evaluate the consistency and physical interpretability of the model's drivers. The research focuses on Yilan County, Taiwan, a region characterized by complex hydrological responses to extreme weather events. Preliminary findings indicate that both current and antecedent inundation depth data are the most critical predictors. Additionally, specific rainfall observations from localized gauging stations significantly enhance the model's predictive performance. By providing a transparent framework for understanding how different factors contribute to inundation, this research offers valuable insights for developing more reliable and interpretable forecasting systems, bridging the gap between algorithmic optimization and physical understanding.

presentations.presentation_title: AI Forecast of Internal Solitary Waves in the South China Sea
presentations.abstract: The generation and propagation of internal solitary waves (ISWs) are highly complex processes, making their numerical simulation computationally expensive. In this study, ISWs are simulated using CROCO, a non-hydrostatic hydrodynamic model, which was validated against field measurements. Based on the Hovmöller diagram, ISWs are traced to their source, revealing that internal tides are generated at the eastern ridge during peaks in eastward tidal currents. These waves then propagate westward, evolving into ISWs. Therefore, the stratification that affects wave propagation, as well as the tidal information near the source zone, are used as the input parameters. Then, the arrival time of ISWs in the hydrodynamic model at various gridded stations across the South China Sea is used to train an AI model based on Back-Propagating Neural Network (BPN). By partitioning the simulation data into training and validation sets, the model achieved a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.15 hours during training and 0.17 hours during validation. This approach enables prompt and accurate ISW arrival time forecasting without the computational burden of full hydrodynamic simulations.

presentations.presentation_title: A Quantitative Framework Linking Typhoon Track Patterns and Rainfall Temporal Characteristics in Taiwan
presentations.abstract: Typhoons play a dominant role in shaping rainfall over Taiwan, with rainfall characteristics modulated by track patterns, translation speed, and complex topography. An integrated analysis of rainfall temporal distributions combined with typhoon track clusters provides direct insight into the spatiotemporal evolution of typhoon rainfall, which is highly relevant to disaster mitigation and water resources management. Building on existing classifications of typhoon track patterns, this study analyzes Dlandfalling typhoons affecting Taiwan during 1950–2024 using station-based hourly rainfall records to characterize rainfall temporal distributions. Time-series similarity measures with flexible temporal alignment are used in combination with hierarchical clustering to identify typical rainfall hyetographs. The optimal number of clusters is objectively determined using within-cluster variance criteria. A correspondence matrix and statistical tests are used to quantify the linkage between typhoon track patterns and rainfall temporal characteristics. Physical interpretations are then provided with respect to storm translation speed, topographic effects, and large-scale circulation influences. The results reveal a quantitative linkage between typhoon track patterns and rainfall temporal characteristics in Taiwan, which may be useful for pattern-based extended-range rainfall prediction.

presentations.presentation_title: Optimizing Turbulence Modulation in Multi-phase Model for Sediment Transport: an Rbf Neural Network Approach
presentations.institution: Department of Marine Environment and Engineering, National Sun Yat-sen University
presentations.abstract: Standard two-equation turbulence closures, based on the Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes method (RANS), have been shown to overestimate turbulent kinetic energy in surf zones. Employing a Reynolds Stress Model (RSM) to determine all components of the Reynolds stress effectively mitigates this overestimation. This study integrates a RANS-based multiphase flow model with a stress-ω turbulence closure, specifically accounting for the effects of sediment on Reynolds stress (turbulence modulation). A Radial Basis Function Neural Network (RBFNN) is adopted as a surrogate optimizer, enabling the identification of optimal parameters in turbulence modulation terms with minimal simulations. For oscillating boundary layer flows, this method not only avoids excessive turbulence generation during the deceleration phase but also yields velocity profiles consistent with documented experimental data for sheet flows. Sensitivity analysis indicates that the correlation coefficients associated with turbulence modulation exert a significant effect on the computational results.

presentations.presentation_title: A Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Oceanographic Super-resolution: Integrating SVDNN with Residual U-Net Correction
presentations.abstract: Regional marine forecasting typically utilizes global forecasts as boundary conditions for hydrodynamic models to generate high-resolution ocean fields. However, such dynamic downscaling remains computationally expensive. To address this limitation, we propose a computationally efficient hybrid deep learning framework. This model super-resolves key hydrodynamic variables including horizontal and vertical velocities and sea surface elevation across the seas around Taiwan, effectively mapping coarse-resolution inputs from the Copernicus Marine Service (CMEMS) with the high-resolution regional dynamics captured by Central Weather Administration (CWA) simulations.The framework employs a Singular Value Decomposition-based Neural Network (SVDNN), where SVD is first used to reduce the dimensionality of the high-dimensional dataset, retaining the dominant mode ranks and a neural network model is then trained to map the compressed modal coefficients of the coarse-resolution data to those of the fine-resolution target. This step provides a high-fidelity baseline that captures the dominant large-scale dynamics and global flow patterns. To further enhance the reconstruction and recover high-frequency spatial features lost during dimensionality reduction, a U-Net architecture is incorporated within a residual learning framework (Residual U-Net). By minimizing this residual and superimposing it onto the baseline approximation, the proposed framework substantially reduces reconstruction error and improves the spatial fidelity of localized oceanographic structures.

presentations.presentation_title: Accurate and Physically-consistent AI Approach for Satellite-derived SST Reconstruction
presentations.abstract: Rapid advances in satellite and remote sensing technologies have made large volumes of oceanic data accessible, facilitating comprehensive analyses and a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics of the ocean. Among these data, sea surface temperature (SST) plays a crucial role in climate systems, weather patterns, and marine ecosystems, as it reflects the energy exchange between the ocean and the atmosphere. However, compared with in-situ observations, satellite-based infrared remote sensing faces a major challenge from atmospheric interference, particularly cloud cover. In this study, we utilize the SST retrievals accessible from Himawari-9 and then propose an accurate and physically-consistent AI approach to reconstruct daily SSTs in both cloud-covered and cloud-free regions. Under this framework, a Radial Basis Function Neural Network (RBFNN) which fully satisfies the advection-diffusion processes of environmental fluids is employed to learn and estimate SST from temporal and spatial perspectives. Overall, the novel TS-RBFNN has demonstrated excellent performance in full-domain SST reconstruction, achieving a significant improvement up to 60% compared to conventional statistical methods, such as Data Interpolation Empirical Orthogonal Functions (DINEOF). Furthermore, an extension of the proposed approach from daily to hourly SSTs reconstruction will also be presented.

presentations.presentation_title: Machine-learning-based Diagnostics of Sub-seasonal Progression of the Western North Pacific Monsoon and Extreme Rainfall
presentations.institution: National Science and Technology Center for Disaster Reduction
presentations.abstract: During July to early August 2025, Taiwan experienced a prolong period of heavy rainfall associated with multiple typhoons and a long-lasting heavy rainfall event occurring at the end of July, which led to an unusual flood event over southwestern Taiwan. These events coincided with the uncommon persistent monsoon trough over the western North Pacific (WNP), highlighting the need for a robust diagnostic tool to characterize monsoon evolution.In this study, we apply a machine-learning-based seasonal identification technique to diagnose the progression of the WNP summer monsoon. The proposed method employs a deep learning framework combining feature extraction and similarity comparison to objectively identify sub-seasonal progression.Applying this technique to the period 1979–2024 demonstrates that the diagnosed monsoon onset and withdrawal timings are consistent with those reported in previous studies, confirming the capability of the method to capture both the timing and progression of the WNP monsoon. When applied to 2025, the one-dimensional seasonal sequence reveals an anomalously prolonged circulation state corresponding to climatological pentads 42–43 during July to early August 2025.We further adopted the composite analyses based on all pentads that were identified as pentads 42–43 in the last 44 years to investigate the climatological characteristics of those pentads. Multi-scale diagnostics further show that these pentads are characterized by a pronounced monsoon trough extending across Taiwan and adjacent seas, enhanced low-pressure activity, and increased tropical cyclone occurrence. These large-scale circulation features collectively create a favorable environment for extreme rainfall occurrence in Taiwan.

presentations.presentation_title: Establishment of Extreme Wind Speed Estimation Methods for Power Transmission Towers Under Climate Change Scenarios
presentations.abstract: Traditional extreme wind speed estimation for power system infrastructure relies heavily on the assumption of climate stationarity and uses long-term historical observation data. However, as highlighted in the IPCC AR6 and the Taiwan Climate Change Scientific Report 2024, the frequency of intense tropical cyclones and the magnitude of peak gusts are projected to increase significantly, even as the total number of typhoons may decline. These non-stationary trends, characterized by High Impact and Low Probability (HILP) events, pose a severe threat to the structural integrity of power transmission towers, particularly those situated in Taiwan’s complex mountainous terrain. This study presents a systematic framework for estimating extreme wind speed under various climate scenarios to enhance power grid resilience. The methodology integrates international ensemble climate model data with a dual-tier downscaling approach. First, a mesoscale simulation using the Taiwan Weather Research and Forecasting (TWRF) model is conducted at a 3-km horizontal resolution to capture typhoon tracks and intensities. Subsequently, microscale Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) modeling is employed at a 10-meter resolution to account for local topographic speed-up effects. To ensure the reliability of these simulations, the research uses Doppler LiDAR vertical wind profiling and scale-model wind-tunnel experiments for validation and bias correction. The present work establishes a probabilistic extreme value estimation method that combines historical records with simulated future events. The primary outcome is a standardized data product providing long-return-period design wind speeds and uncertainty indices. These outputs serve as critical inputs for Resource Adequacy (RA) planning, Optimal Power Flow (OPF) scheduling, and Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA) within a "prepare–mitigate–respond–recover" resilience framework. By bridging the gap between climate science and structural engineering, this research provides a robust scientific basis for updating wind-resistant building codes and prioritizing infrastructure investments to safeguard essential energy services against future extreme weather risks.

presentations.presentation_title: Interactive Nature of Recent Extreme Atmospheric Heatwaves around Japan with Marine Heatwaves
presentations.abstract: In the last three consequetive summers, Japan underwent unprecedented heatwaves that occurred concurrently with extremely high sea-surface temperature (SST) around Japan as well as along a midlatitude ocean front across the North Pacific. This presentation offers an overview of the interactive nature of the atmospheric heatwaves and extreme warmth of the ocean. In 2023 and 2024, a striking poleward meander of the Kuroshio Extension (KE) caused extremely high SST and subsurface temperatures off the east coast of northern Japan. These marine heatwaves (MHWs) acted to sustain the atmospheric heatwaves over northern and eastern Japan, as suggested by amplified surface air temperature (SAT) anomalies and even stronger warm anomalies in the subsurface ocean. Both enhanced insolation due to reduced low-level clouds and increased clear-sky greenhouse effect acted to reinforce the extremely high SAT and SST as positive feedback. In 2024 summer, Okinawa also suffered from an unprecedented heatwave, which was possibly reinforced by a MHW south of Japan initiated in late June under profoundly increased insolation after the termination of the Baiu period. In addition, a possible impact of pronounced positive SST anomalies along the midlatitude ocean fronts across the North Pacific and Atlantic on the large-scale extreme tropospheric warmth in 2024 is also discussed.This work is supported in part by JST through COI-NEXT "ClimCORE" (JPMJPF2013).

presentations.presentation_title: Evolution of Outdoor Thermal Stress Under Heatwaves: Comparative Analysis Based on Multiple Indices Over Mainland China
presentations.institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: As global warming intensifies, heatwaves (HWs) are occurring with increasing frequency. However, the extent of the synergistic interaction between outdoor thermal stress (TS) and HWs, as well as their climatic drivers, has yet to be fully understood. his study investigates the spatiotemporal patterns and climatic determinants of TS across China from 1990 to 2017, using historical meteorological data and a suite of composite thermal stress indices. Results reveal no significant trend in TS during HWs, while an increasing trend is observed during non-HW conditions. Despite smaller temperature variability, southern regions experience greater increases in thermal sensation than northern regions during HWs, as small changes in absolute temperature correspond to large increases in temperature percentiles. Furthermore, the response of TS to climatic background is regionally dependent. Hotter regions generally exhibited a smaller increase in TS. In dry areas, TS intensification was positively correlated with increased precipitation, whereas this trend reversed in transitional climate zones and remained stable in wet areas. These changes in TS are primarily driven by the changes in air temperature (T a ) across different climate contexts. A key finding is that the intensification of the urban heat island (UHI) effect mitigated the rise in TS within urban areas specifically during HWs. Additionally, different thermal stress indices responded variably to climatic drivers. The widely used wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) showed the smallest increase with rising T a , suggesting it may underestimate thermal stress relative to other metrics. These findings offer critical insights into the spatiotemporal dynamics of thermal stress in China, providing a scientific foundation for developing targeted heat adaptation strategies to mitigate the impacts of heatwaves.

presentations.presentation_title: Projecting the Morbidity Burden of Mental and Behavioral Disorders Associated with Increasing Humid Heat in Shanghai
presentations.abstract: Residents of low-latitude megacities face growing vulnerability to humid-heat stress under urbanization and global warming, yet limited research has assessed the morbidity burden of mental and behavioral disorders (MBDs) linked to humid-heat exposures in these cities. Here we quantify the hospital admissions of MBDs in Shanghai, a megacity of over 25 million inhabitants, attributable to humid heat, and project future burdens under various greenhouse gas (GHG)-emission and population scenarios. Humid heat drives a higher morbidity burden than high temperature alone, especially in humid-heat nights. Without population change, the humid-heat-related morbidity burden of MBDs would increase by 68.2% (95% empirical confidence interval 56.7%–81.6%) under the highest-GHG-emission scenario by the 2090s, while 8,465 (95% empirical confidence interval 6,928–10,053) cases would be avoided by reducing emissions to the lowest pathway. With projected population decline, the attributable hospital admissions will decrease toward century’s end. These findings highlight the benefit of GHG mitigation in reducing the growing MBD risks posed by extreme humid heat.

presentations.presentation_title: The Critical Role of Internal Climate Variability and Extremes in Climate–economic Damage Attribution
presentations.abstract: Climate–economic research increasingly seeks to understand how global warming will affect equitable economic development, guiding strategies for mitigation and adaptation. Yet attributing economic damages directly to climate change remains challenging, as internal climate variability and climate and weather extremes can mask or amplify long‑term temperature trends, alter regional trajectories, and generate highly heterogeneous impacts across countries and sectors. Using the Max Planck Institute Grand Ensemble (MPI‑GE), I quantify the uncertainty in climate‑related economic damage arising from internal variability and extremes. I calculate bias‑corrected, population‑weighted mean temperatures for each country, link them to observed temperature–growth relationships, and use these to estimate damages. This framework allows me to separate the forced climate signal from internal variability and capture a wide range of extreme temperature evolutions under global warming. I find that detecting a clear climate‑damage signal in the historical period is hindered by a marked rise in uncertainty from the early 1990s to the early 2010s, even as global temperature variability remains stable. Vulnerability is greatest in cold high‑latitude and warm low‑latitude regions lying outside the median climate‑optimal zone. These findings underscore the critical role of variability and extremes in shaping the detectability, magnitude, and spatial patterns of climate‑related economic damage. Building on this attribution study, I place these results in the broader context of Earth System Model (ESM) and Integrated Assessment Model (IAM) applications to global and regional economies. I examine limitations of current climate models in representing extremes, highlight advances in global kilometre‑scale modelling, and discuss new IAM designs that incorporate two‑way coupling between human and natural systems. Integrating cutting‑edge climate science with economic analysis, I aim to provide key insights to guide local adaptation planning and inform global policy, adaptation, and mitigation strategies.
presentations.session_title: Changing Heatwave Characteristics in a Warming World: Mechanisms, Predictability, and Impacts on Society and Environment

presentations.presentation_title: From Climate to Health: Recent Progress in Heatwave Research.
presentations.abstract: Heatwaves are loosely defined as prolonged periods of excessive heat, with definitions varying across disciplines and individual studies. Climate-focused research has demonstrated that the intensity, frequency and duration of heatwaves has increased almost everywhere in the world since at least the 1950s. Moreover, extensive global research has provided a sound understanding of both the natural and human influences on the frequency and intensity of heatwaves. Projected heatwave trends will continue during the 21 st century, driven by the amount of atmospheric carbon. Moreover, even in a net zero world, heatwaves will likely be more severe and more frequent relative to current conditions. Across the world, heatwaves are associated with significantly increased mortality rates and place great strain on human health services, with these impacts projected to intensify as heatwaves increase. The combination of temperature and humidity is particularly dangerous, as high values of both inhibit cooling via evaporation, further exacerbating the effect of extreme heat on the human body. There are many metrics employed to determine dangerous levels of combined heat and humidity, with a wet-bulb threshold of 35 o C commonly used to describe the up-most limit of human survivability. However, recent interdisciplinary research has demonstrated that based on human physiology, age, and whether a person is seeking shelter or is outside, the limit of survivability can be much lower.This talk will explore our understanding of what drives heatwaves, the attribution of recent significant events to human influence, future projections of heatwaves under enhanced climate change and net zero, as well as recent and future events in the context of human physiology over different climates and cities. Lastly, it is shown that that such conditions occur well before a wet-bulb value of 35 o C is reached, demonstrating that this theorised threshold significantly underestimates the effect of heat and humidity on the human body.
presentations.session_title: Changing Heatwave Characteristics in a Warming World: Mechanisms, Predictability, and Impacts on Society and Environment

presentations.presentation_title: Influence of the Sea-surface Temperature in the Coastal Region on the Extreme Heat Events in Tokyo
presentations.abstract: Recent extreme heat events from 2015 to 2023 in Tokyo were examined, focusing on wet-bulb temperature as a measure of heat stress. Analyses from the Japan Meteorological Agency stations reveal that Tokyo has had almost the most frequent extreme heat events in the main island of Japan. Long-term analyses since the 1990s have shown that the daily maximum wet-bulb temperature in Tokyo during the summer has increased in recent years. The days with extremely high wet-bulb temperature do not coincide with those of extremely high air temperature. According to composite analyses from a mesoscale objective analysis, humidity is low due to dry foehn caused by northwesterly downslope winds on extremely high air temperature days. On the other hand, on days with extremely high wet-bulb temperature, moist air arrives with intensified surface southwesterly winds along the northwestern periphery of the North Pacific subtropical high, resulting in the extreme heat events in Tokyo. In addition, analyses of sea-surface temperature (SST) data obtained by in-situ observation revealed that wet-bulb temperature in Tokyo correlates with the SST in Tokyo Bay when surface southwesterly winds prevail. It appears that the SST confines the upper limit of wet-bulb temperature in the coastal region. Moreover, by comparing the meteorological conditions and the SST, it is implied that consecutive hot and sunny days warm the sea surface. These results stress the importance of considering the interaction between the atmospheric conditions and the sea surface when projecting future heat environments in the coastal regions.
presentations.session_title: Changing Heatwave Characteristics in a Warming World: Mechanisms, Predictability, and Impacts on Society and Environment

presentations.presentation_title: Marine Heatwave Amplification of the Record-breaking 2023 East Asian Hot-humid Extreme
presentations.abstract: The summer of 2023 in East Asia was characterized by record-breaking compound hot-humid extremes, accompanied by an unprecedented marine heatwave in the surrounding oceans. Such humid-heat extremes pose severe risks to human health, yet the quantitative influence of marine heatwaves on land heatwaves remains poorly understood.Here we investigate the impact of the 2023 marine heatwave on the East Asian summer heatwave using a set of regional atmospheric model experiments. Focusing on the peak hot and humid months of July-September, the simulations show that anomalously warm sea surface temperatures significantly amplified both surface air temperature and humidity over land, intensifying the atmospheric heatwave beyond the effects of background large-scale circulation anomalies. The MHW influence on air temperature is primarily mediated through radiative effects associated with changes in clouds and water vapor. Despite a damping effect on the western North Pacific subtropical high, the overall heatwave intensity is enhanced. We also examine the dependence of the marine heatwave’s impact on the atmospheric conditions.Assessment using wet-bulb globe temperature indicates that the marine heatwave accounts for approximately 20-50% of the increased severity and prolonged duration of hot-humid conditions across East Asia. Furthermore, recent trends in ocean warming have made this effect even stronger. Our findings underscore the key role of ocean variability and air-sea interactions in shaping summer atmospheric heatwaves in East Asia, highlighting a unique process in this humid, low-cloud-abundant maritime region, and suggesting the importance of marine heatwaves for improving seasonal prediction and heat-risk preparedness in a rapidly warming climate.
