presentations.presentation_title: A Study on the Standardization and Application of Graphic Symbols by Disaster Type
presentations.abstract: This study aims to standardize disaster-type graphic symbols based on Korea’s disaster classification system under the Framework Act on the Management of Disasters and Safety (and its related regulations) and to propose a draft Korean Industrial Standard (KS) for disaster information communication. Relevant domestic and international laws, regulations, and graphic symbol standards (e.g., KS, ISO) were reviewed. From a set developed in prior research, 65 symbols were refined and selected through comparison with similar symbols in current use, expert surveys, and a comprehension test adapted from ISO 9186-1. The study frames these as “disaster safety information symbols (or signs)” and proposes a draft KS specification including a coding and reference numbering scheme, a classification system, and a standardized description format. Application guidelines are suggested for multiple media—such as disaster safety portals, disaster broadcasting, early warning and emergency text messages, public signage, educational materials, and AAC tools—with attention to vulnerable populations, to improve the consistency and accessibility of disaster information.
presentations.session_title: General Session

presentations.presentation_title: Development of Disaster-type Graphic Symbols for Enhanced Disaster Information Visualization and Response Support
presentations.abstract: As climate change and social-environmental transitions intensify, the frequency and complexity of large-scale disasters are increasing worldwide. Under these conditions, the importance of visual communication for delivering disaster information quickly and intuitively has gained increasing attention. However, current disaster information systems remain predominantly text-based, resulting in low risk perception and limited public comprehension. Moreover, inconsistencies in visual representation across institutions hinder effective information delivery during emergencies. This study aims to develop disaster-type graphic symbols as an effective medium to support disaster information visualization and disaster response. Based on Korea’s official disaster classification system, relevant laws, institutional frameworks, and existing disaster safety symbols were systematically reviewed. Through expert consultation and stakeholder workshops, the design direction was established, and a final set of 65 disaster-type graphic symbols was derived through preference surveys. The developed symbols emphasize inter-type distinctiveness, visual intuitiveness, and applicability across diverse communication channels. This research provides foundational resources for the standardization of disaster information visualization and the advancement of disaster communication systems, contributing to improved situational awareness, public safety, and societal resilience.
presentations.session_title: General Session

presentations.presentation_title: Analysis on the Current Status of the Term ‘Geoeducation’ Using NLP Techniques
presentations.abstract: This study aims to clarify the conceptual scope of geoscience education, a term that has been used with diverse meanings in research on the educational utilization of geoheritage and georesources. The dataset consists of 3,772 geopark- and geoheritage-related studies collected from the Web of Science database between 1978 and 2025. To efficiently analyze this large corpus and systematically examine the multidimensional contexts in which the term has been applied, natural language processing (NLP) techniques were employed. Specifically, topic modeling was used to extract latent thematic structures from bibliographic text data. Furthermore, the extracted topics were visualized in a two-dimensional space to examine patterns of topic cohesion and separation, leading to the following findings. First, in studies related to geoparks and geoheritage, the concept of geoscience education can be broadly classified into three major categories. (1) Geoscience education as an abstract concept that emphasizes the geological value of geoheritage itself and advocates the necessity of its educational utilization; (2) geoscience education as a teaching–learning concept that focuses on learning outcomes (cognitive, skill-based, and affective domains) derived from educational activities using geoheritage, rather than on the geological characteristics of the heritage itself; and (3) geoscience education as an educational program concept that refers to activities developed by geoheritage-related institutions in response to visitors’ purposes and needs. These three categories are distributed across different analytical levels. Second, the research domains of geoscience education and geopark certification showed little spatial overlap, indicating that studies in these two fields have developed independently without close integration. The results of this study further suggest that research on geoscience education has been conducted using these three conceptual meanings interchangeably, and that none of the three conceptual categories of geoscience education is necessarily regarded as a critical factor in the geopark certification process.

presentations.presentation_title: Geomorphological Characteristics of Maruhata, Terraced Fields Unique to Fukue Island, and Their Relationship with Social Infrastructure and Ecosystems
presentations.institution: Ecological Engineering Labolatory, Department of Civil Engineering, Graduate School of Engineering, Kyushu University
presentations.abstract: Japan is experiencing advanced population decline and aging, which poses serious challenges to the sustainability of rural regions. At the same time, global efforts to reduce CO₂ emissions have increased interest in alternatives to conventional gray infrastructure. In this context, green infrastructure has attracted attention for its potential contributions to local industries, biodiversity conservation, and disaster risk reduction. However, quantitative evaluations of traditional rural landscapes as green infrastructure remain limited.This study focuses on Fukue Island, located in the southern Goto Islands of western Japan, where distinctive circular terraced fields known as Maruhata are well preserved. Maruhata are distributed across the Fukue area, Miiraku Town, and Tomie Town. In Miiraku Town, Maruhata are typically surrounded by camellia (Camellia japonica) forests, whereas those in the Fukue area and Tomie Town are commonly supported by stone retaining walls. This spatial variation provides an opportunity to examine different landscape-based stabilization structures using quantitative data.Topographic characteristics of Maruhata were analyzed using elevation data to quantify slope gradients, field areas, and surface continuity. At the foot of volcanic landforms in Miiraku Town, Maruhata exhibited gentle average slopes of approximately 1.5% and field areas of about 2,727.54 m². In the Fukue area, slopes ranged from approximately 1.5% to 2.0%, and field areas were about 2,526.93 m². Furthermore, adjacent Maruhata terraces in both Miiraku Town and the Fukue area showed nearly identical slope gradients and a continuous surface geometry.These results suggest that camellia forests and stone retaining walls may have been introduced onto originally continuous volcanic landforms to enhance ground stability and reduce soil runoff. In particular, camellia forests in Miiraku Town are likely to function as natural retaining structures that limit soil movement from terraced fields. This study demonstrates the potential value of Maruhata and camellia forests as components of green infrastructure and highlights the importance of quantitative geomorphological analysis in evaluating traditional agricultural landscapes.

presentations.presentation_title: Social Contact Reshapes Topographic Constraints on Lexical Convergence
presentations.abstract: Language maps shared concepts onto words through repeated social coordination grounded in real-world experience. Because human experience is embedded in physical environments, populations living in different geographic zones may develop distinct patterns of lexical convergence. At the same time, increasing levels of social contact—driven by population growth, urbanization, and digital communication—may reshape or override geographic constraints on naming conventions.Here, we examine how physical geography and social contact environments jointly shape population-level lexical convergence, operationalized as name agreement in picture-naming tasks. We analyzed publicly available naming data covering 500 visual concepts across 32 languages, using linear mixed-effects models to test the effects of language family, topographic diversity, population density, urbanization, cyberization, and historical word age.We find that name agreement varies systematically across languages and is predicted by both language family and topographic diversity. Crucially, after controlling for language family, the effect of topography is strongly modulated by social contact environments. In regions with low population density, greater topographic diversity is associated with higher name agreement, suggesting that geographic isolation promotes convergence on shared naming conventions. In contrast, in regions with high population density, greater topographic diversity predicts lower name agreement, consistent with increased lexical differentiation in socially dense environments. Cyberization further reshapes these patterns by attenuating the negative effects of topographic diversity on name agreement. Moreover, this rewriting effect depends on word age: for older words, high levels of cyberization render topographic effects negligible, whereas for newer words, cyberization reverses the effect, making topographic diversity a positive predictor of lexical convergence.Together, these findings demonstrate that population-level lexical convergence emerges from the interaction between physical geography and social contact environments, highlighting how shared linguistic representations are shaped by collective cognitive coordination rather than geography alone.

presentations.presentation_title: Examining Social Vulnerability of the Tribals to Climate Extremes in Jharkhand, India
presentations.abstract: The escalating incidence of Climate Extremes in India poses a significant threat to socially and economically marginalized communities. Among them, the tribal population of Jharkhand remains particularly vulnerable owing to its high dependence on natural resources, limited adaptive capacity, and socioeconomic exclusion. Thus, an attempt has been made to investigate the underlying socioeconomic factors that enhance the region's susceptibility to climate extremes. This study evaluated the Social Vulnerability of the tribes to climate extremes across Jharkhand’s districts by constructing a composite Social Vulnerability Index (SoVI) using two distinct quantitative approaches: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Shannon’s Entropy Method. The methodological framework integrates 12 indicators and 30 variables representing exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity. PCA reduced the indicators into seven principal components explaining 68.4% of the variance, capturing critical aspects of economic disadvantage, demographic dependency, and infrastructural deficit. In contrast, the Shannon Entropy method assigns objective weights based on indicator entropy values, independent of inter-variable correlations. Comparative spatial analysis revealed distinct vulnerability patterns, with high-vulnerability clusters concentrated in southern (SoVI > 0.40) and western (SoVI > 0.56) districts, where ST populations exceeded 40% and coincided with flood- and drought-prone zones. The results highlight pronounced inter-district disparities driven by low adaptive capacity and heavy reliance on climate-sensitive livelihoods. This study contributes methodologically by demonstrating the relative strengths and limitations of PCA and entropy-based weighting for multidimensional vulnerability assessments in tribal contexts. The findings provide critical insights for policymakers to target adaptation interventions and equitable resource allocation in climate-sensitive tribal regions.

presentations.presentation_title: Preliminary Geomorphosite Assessment of Siargao Island, Philippines, Using a Modified Evaluation Model
presentations.abstract: Geoparks are territories of exceptional geological importance that integrate geoscience education, conservation, and geotourism. They comprise geosites of scientific, aesthetic, cultural, and economic value, with geomorphologically significant locations identified as geomorphosites. As of July 2025, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) has designated 229 Global Geoparks across more than 50 countries, each subject to revalidation every four years. This study evaluates Siargao Island, a major tourist destination in the Philippines, as a potential geopark. Potential geosites were mapped and assessed mainly using a Geographic Information System (GIS)-based approach, considering their scientific, intrinsic, educational, cultural, aesthetic, conservation, and economic attributes. Preliminary analyses of seven geosites across four municipalities indicate that only three sites—Litik Maasin River, Tayangban Cave, and Magpupungko Rock Formation and Tidal Pools (all in Pilar)—currently implement geotourism policies, contributing to their higher geomorphosite rankings. Furthermore, six of the seven sites are situated within or adjacent to water bodies, underscoring the close interconnection between the island’s geotourism and hydrogeological setting. As one of the few geopark-focused studies conducted in the Philippines, this research promotes sustainable geotourism development in Siargao and supports its potential nomination as a UNESCO Global Geopark. This research was supported by the Basic Science Research Program through the National Research Foundation of Korea (RS-2019-NR040076 and RS-2025-25426615) funded by the Ministry of Education (2025).

presentations.presentation_title: Assessing Climate Variability and Land Surface Vulnerability in the Upper Chambal Basin, India
presentations.abstract: Environmental degradation driven by changing climatic patterns and land deterioration poses major challenges to semi-arid regions by impacting water cycle dynamics, the edaphic system and landscape resilience. The Chambal basin, which is environmentally fragile and climatically unstable, has limited studies integrating climatic variability, soil erosion, and land surface assessment. This study aims to assess how climatic variability influences soil erosion dynamics and land surface stability in the Chambal basin. It used a mixed-method approach, including the Modified Mann-Kendall test to detect trends, RUSLE-based modelling to estimate soil erosion, and the Bare Soil Index to map bare soil exposure for 2001, 2012, and 2024. The findings revealed that the Modified MK Z-values for rainfall ranged from −0.83 to 3.94, indicating heterogeneous rainfall variability, including both declining and increasing rainfall pockets and erratic rainfall zones. While minimum temperature shows substantial variability (Z = 2.70–4.08), especially in the southwest and northeast, maximum temperature shows an increasing, spatially consistent trend with low variability (Z = 0.33–0.75). The estimates of soil erosion vary from 0 to 11.93 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, with over 98% of the basin showing very low erosion (<5 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹), but only a few steep, riparian, and dissected areas exhibit slight to moderate erosion. The percentage of bare soil exposure decreased dramatically from 11.56% in 2001 to 9.53% in 2012 and then to 4.89% in 2024, showing better land cover conditions. The results indicate that, despite increasing climatic stress in the Chambal basin, the terrain remains mostly stable, with localised erosion vulnerability. These findings are important for planning for erosion reduction, managing watersheds responsively to climate change, and enhancing the basin's environmental resilience.

presentations.presentation_title: High-Resolution 3-D Tomography of the Ionospheric Responses Over Japan Following an Earthquake
presentations.abstract: The sudden shaking of the Earth's surface caused by earthquakes can disrupt the ionosphere through atmospheric waves and generate traveling ionospheric disturbances (TIDs). However, detailed information regarding these TIDs has primarily been confined to fragmented insights into the horizontal two-dimensional structure. Owing to Japan’s dense network of Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receivers, high-resolution three-dimensional (3-D) imaging of ionospheric responses to earthquakes can be achieved using computerized ionospheric tomography (CIT). This technique has proven effective in capturing the 3-D dynamics and morphology of TIDs associated with the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake (Mw 7.5) (Fu et al., 2025). In that study, we not only confirmed that the observed electron density perturbations were driven by acoustic waves launched from the earthquake, but also revealed nonlinear acoustic-wave propagation in the ionosphere, accompanied with the presence of multiple acoustic wave sources along the fault. Building on these advances, we aim to apply this approach to additional earthquake events to further improve our understanding of ionospheric responses to seismic activity. Reference:Fu, W., Otsuka, Y., Ssessanga, N. et al. Unveiling the vertical ionospheric responses following the 2024 Noto Peninsula Earthquake with an ultra-dense GNSS network. Earth Planets Space 77, 77 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1186/s40623-025-02211-y

presentations.presentation_title: GNSS-TEC observations of near- and far-field ionospheric disturbances associated with the 2025 Jul. 29 Mw8.8 Kamchatka earthquake
presentations.abstract: Large earthquakes excite atmospheric waves and cause coseismic ionospheric disturbances (CsID). They can be observed as changes in total electron contents (TEC) using ground-based receivers of global navigation satellite system (GNSS). Here we report multi-GNSS observations of CsID of the 2025 Jul. 29 M w 8.8 Kamchatka Peninsula megathrust earthquake, at stations in various focal distances; the SKUR station just above the ruptured fault, dense arrays of GNSS receivers in Japan (GEONET) and Taiwan (GDMS) 2000-4000 km from the epicenter, and >4,000 km stations in the Pacific Basin. The receiver at the SKUR station, at Severo-Kurilsk, tracked all GNSS constellations and recorded near-field CsID at ionospheric piercing points (IPP) in the distance range of 0-600 km, with >20 GNSS satellites. It was found that the TEC data from SKUR with high elevation satellites (i.e., with IPP close to the fault) recorded clear changes of TEC immediately before the earthquake. With far-field stations we observed two different components, one propagating southward at the acoustic wave speed (~1 km/s) and the other propagating toward a wide range of azimuths at the Rayleigh wave speed (~3.5 km/s). The former was seen at IPP within ~2,000 km of the epicenter. The latter signals were clearly tracked beyond 4,000 km and became invisible around 6,000 km. These CsID signals are composed of the initial strong pulse and the subsequent wave train with a period of ~4 minutes lasting for more than six hours. We investigate the origin of the wave train by comparing them with high-rate crustal movements of a few GNSS stations at various epicentral distances. We could not find the component propagating at the internal gravity wave speed.

presentations.presentation_title: Automatic Ionospheric Imaging of the Seismic Fault Slip
presentations.institution: Earthquake Research Institute, The University of Tokyo
presentations.abstract: Can co-seismic ionospheric disturbances (CSID) be used to characterize earthquake fault slip? To date, only two studies addressed this question, focusing on the 2004 Sumatra-Andaman and the 2011 Tohoku-Oki earthquakes. In this work, we present a novel method for automatic ionospheric imaging of seismic fault slip using Total Electron Content (TEC) data. The evolution of CSID can be divided into two phases: initial anomaly generation and its propagation from the source area. A key challenge is to separate these phases, as only the initial anomaly is suitable to retrieve earthquake parameters such as magnitude, fault length, and width. Our method uses the earliest CSID arrivals to detect the anomaly and image the seismic fault slip. We use the locations and amplitudes of the first arrivals as well as the dTEC/dt parameter to constrain the geometry of the rupture fault. To develop and evaluate this method, we collected TEC data from 20 earthquakes (successfully imaged 11) obtained by Japan’s GNSS network, which offers the unique spatio-temporal resolution required for imaging. We assess the necessary conditions for effective application and compare the method’s performance under different earthquake characteristics (magnitude, focal mechanism), different non-seismic factor conditions (geomagnetic field-neutral wave alignment, satellite geometry of sounding, background level of ionisation) and different temporal (30s vs. 1s) and spatial (sparse vs. dense networks) resolutions. The estimations of horizontal dimensions of the fault by the ionospheric data show a good agreement with those obtained by traditional approaches (e.g., seismic and tsunami methods). Therefore, GNSS-TEC data can complement a set of conventional/standard tools (e.g., seismometers, tsunami meters) to study the earthquake source area. Besides, potentially, the resulting evaluations of vertical displacements and their dimensions enable near-real-time (NRT; within 10–12 minutes from the onset) imaging of earthquakes by TEC data for rapid tsunami risk assessment.

presentations.presentation_title: Identifying Coseismic Surface Uplift Distribution of the 2025 Myanmar Earthquake Using Ionospheric Disturbances
presentations.abstract: The Sagaing fault, a major active strike-slip boundary between the Indian and Sunda plates, ruptured on 28 March 2025 to produce the longest Mw 7.7 earthquake event recorded so far, with unusual length of ~480 km (Shengji Wei et al. 2025). The rupture initiated bilaterally at the epicentre (~22°N ~95.92°E) ~06:20:52 UTC and propagated with subshear velocity (lower than the shear wave velocity) in the north and with supershear velocity (higher than the shear wave velocity) in the south (He et al. 2025).Due to the lack of continuous Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) observations close to the earthquake source, the measurements of coseismic crustal movements are not available and also due to the strike-slip nature of the event, it is difficult to identify vertical movements from the synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images. We propose here a unique way to identify the distribution of vertical displacements along the rupture by using GNSS-measured total electron content (TEC) data from stations along the India-Myanmar border hundreds of kilometres away from the fault. These GNSS stations are part of the dense Continuously Operating Reference Stations (CORS) network established by Survey of India. We further employ forward numerical simulation approach by considering the identified displacements as sources and effectively reproduce the associated ionospheric disturbances. Results will be discussed in detail during the presentation. References Shengji Wei et al., (2025). Supershear rupture sustained through a thick fault zone in the 2025 M w 7.8 Mandalay earthquake. Science, 390, 468-475 .DOI:10.1126/science.adz2101. He, Z., Zhang, Z., Wang, X., Wang, Z., Sunilkumar, T. C., Xu, X., & Wang, R. (2026). Rupture dynamics of the 2025 Mw 7.7 Myanmar earthquake: A bilateral supershear rupture on unusually long fault superhighway. Geophysical Research Letters, 53, e2025GL118023. https://doi.org/10.1029/2025GL118023.

presentations.presentation_title: On the altitude of GNSS detection of co-seismic ionospheric disturbances
presentations.institution: Institut de physique du globe de Paris, Univesité Paris Cité
presentations.abstract: GNSS-based ionospheric-sounding (GNSS-sounding) allow us to measure total electron content (TEC), which is equal to the number of electrons along the line of site between a satellite and a receiver. Nowadays, the GNSS-sounding is widely used to monitor the ionosphere, and, in particular, to detect ionospheric disturbances generated by earthquakes (Co-Seismic Ionospheric Disturbances, CSID). The main disadvantage of the GNSS-sounding is the imprecise estimate of the exact altitude of initial signal arrival (Hion) of an ionospheric TEC disturbance. From physical principles, the Hion is presumed to be around the altitude of the maximum of ionization, i.e., between 250 km and 400 km, depending on solar, geomagnetic, seasonal, and diurnal conditions. Changing the Hion value changes the geographic coordinates of the observed TEC disturbances, which in turn influences the ability to infer properties about the source of the disturbance. For many applications, the exact value of the Hion is not necessary, whereas it is crucial for the Ionospheric Seismology that uses CSID to find the location of the seismic source, which can also be the source that generates tsunamis. In this work, we present the results of our detailed investigation of the altitude of GNSS-detection of CSID generated by 20 earthquakes with different magnitudes. Our analysis is performed using GNSS-observations and three simulation techniques. We propose that two observation-based methods enable a useful estimate the Hion, and are applicable in near-real-time. We demonstrate that, depending on the GNSS satellite geometry and the fault position, the Hion is different for each line-of-sight, and can vary between 150 and 300 km.
presentations.session_title: Ionospheric Seismology and Volcanology

presentations.presentation_title: A Simulation Study of Atmosphere-ionosphere Variations Associated with Volcanic Eruptions
presentations.abstract: A number of studies have indicated that significant disturbances in the atmosphere and the ionosphere are generated in volcanic eruptions. In the volcanic eruption of Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai in Tonga on 15 January 2022 various kinds of observations have been made, providing us with large amount of data of the atmosphere and the ionosphere. While numerous observational studies have been made, several simulations have also been made to investigate the atmosphere-ionosphere variations driven by the volcanic eruption. The simulation studies have successfully reproduced the global variations of the atmosphere and the ionosphere. Recent theoretical studies also showed that many complicated modes of atmospheric waves in volcanic eruptions can be driven by the volcanic eruptions in the realistic atmosphere. However, some phenomena in the upper atmosphere are yet to be fully understood. Among some outstanding problems we focus on the following processes (1) behavior of Lamb waves in the upper atmosphere, (2) acoustic waves in the upper atmosphere, (3) interaction between different types of atmospheric waves. To better understand those processes, we employed a revised version of the model of Shinagawa and Miyoshi (2024): a coupled model of the nonhydrostatic atmospheric model and the whole atmosphere-ionosphere model GAIA. The simulation results indicate: (1) in the mesosphere-lower thermosphere region, the interaction between thermospheric gravity waves and Lamb waves occurs, (2) ionospheric oscillations are generated through the interaction of Lamb waves and gravity waves in the atmosphere, (3) Lamb wave-like waves in the thermosphere are thermospheric gravity waves with the same phase speed of Lamb waves in the lower atmosphere. We will present and discuss the simulation results by comparing with observations.
presentations.session_title: Ionospheric Seismology and Volcanology

presentations.presentation_title: High-precision Relocation of Deep Low-frequency Earthquakes Beneath Mt. Fuji: Insights Into Deep Fluid-related Fracture System
presentations.abstract: At Mt. Fuji, the time between the onset of shallow precursors and eruption may be short. This highlights the need to detect earlier-stage volcanic signals. Deep low-frequency earthquakes (DLFs) are regarded as among the earliest seismic manifestations of deep magmatic activity. Ikegaya et al. (2025, IAVCEI) classified 3,944 DLFs beneath Mt. Fuji into five waveform groups. All groups had focal mechanisms with volumetric components, and their activity and spatial distributions differ. Some groups show increased activity after the inflation event, suggesting sensitivity to deep magma reservoir pressurization. In this study, we investigate the detailed spatial distribution of DLFs using high-precision hypocenter relocation and examine its relationship with waveform groups. We applied the double-difference method using P- and S-wave arrival times from the Japan Meteorological Agency, supplemented by deep-learning-based automatic phase picks. The uncertainties were evaluated by bootstrap resampling, and events with standard deviations larger than 500 m were excluded. The relocated hypocenters formed a narrow depth distribution, and their epicenters showed a curved structure. Each waveform group is distributed in slightly different locations within this structure. This geometry resembles fracture systems developed above sill-like magma bodies in caldera volcanoes (Mori and McKee, 1987). Previous studies showed that DLFs occur in fluid-rich regions just above the deep magma reservoir (Nakamichi et al., 2007) and exhibit focal mechanisms with volumetric components. Our results suggest that DLFs beneath Mt. Fuji may be associated with fluid- or magma-filled fracture networks developed above the magma reservoir. Activity differences among waveform groups may be associated with subtle differences in their source locations. Therefore, integrating high-precision hypocenter relocation with previously obtained waveform classification and focal mechanism results provides a basis for more detailed monitoring of deep magmatic activity and may contribute to early-stage assessment of volcanic unrest.
presentations.session_title: Ionospheric Seismology and Volcanology

presentations.presentation_title: Seismic Indicators of Magmatic System Sensitivity in Japan: Mt. Fuji Activation and Izu Peninsula Seismicity Changes
presentations.abstract: Mt. Fuji, Japan’s highest mountain and an active volcano, and the eastern Izu Peninsula, a monogenetic volcanic field, are both located near densely populated regions in Japan. These settings provide key natural laboratories where improved monitoring can directly support disaster preparedness. Here we integrate two recent studies to demonstrate how data-driven seismic analyses reveal subtle but societally important changes in volcanic systems. First, we show that Mt. Fuji volcanism was reactivated after the 2011 Japanese large earthquakes (Nanjo et al., 2023). Using a matched-filter approach, we detected deep volcanic low-frequency earthquakes (LFEs) activated following the 2011 M5.9 Shizuoka earthquake at the volcano’s foot, which occurred four days after the 2011 M9 Tohoku megathrust earthquake. The increased LFE rate did not return to pre-event levels, implying a persistent change in the magma system and a high sensitivity to external stress perturbations. Second, we investigate seismicity changes in the eastern Izu Peninsula, where shallow ordinary earthquake swarms occurred in 2006 and 2009 above deeper LFEs (Nanjo et al., 2025). We constructed an LFE catalog for 2005–2020 using matched filtering and applied ETAS-based change-point analyses to both LFEs and ordinary earthquakes. Both datasets show quiescence beginning during or after each swarm, with an earlier onset for shallow earthquakes than for deeper LFEs. Together with limited uplift, these results are consistent with magma intrusion followed by depth-dependent stress relaxation in and around the magma reservoir. We discuss how transferable workflows combining matched-filter detection, ETAS change-point monitoring, and seismic–geodetic interpretation can contribute to a global volcano “collaboratory” aimed at strengthening hazard resilience.

presentations.presentation_title: Analysis of Precursory Seismicity and Transient Changes in the b-value of the Gutenberg-Richter Relation for Near-real-time Volcanic Eruption Forecasting
presentations.institution: Association for the Development of Earthquake Prediction (ADEP)
presentations.abstract: Many volcanoes produce precursory signals before erupting, reflecting hidden subsurface processes. Thus, forecasting efforts rely on detecting statistically significant deviations from the long-term background level of these signals, with seismic data playing a central role.This can be achieved by analyzing the b-value slope of the Gutenberg-Richter magnitude-frequency relation, which reflects the ratio of small to large earthquakes. Spatiotemporal variations in b-value have been linked to processes such as differential stress, thermal gradients, pore pressure changes, and fracture density, all indicators of crustal heterogeneity. In this study, we analyze transient variations in seismicity rate and b-value to identify crustal stress conditions under which seismicity is the most effective for near-real-time eruption forecasting. We selected eight well-monitored volcanoes: Eyjafjallajökull, Fagradalsfjall, Grímsvötn, and Holuhraun (Bárðarbunga) (Iceland); Mauna Loa in Hawaii (USA); and Kirishima, Ontake, and Usu (Japan). First, we compute b-value time series using both the Maximum Likelihood Estimation and b-positive methods. Next, we define red light as instances when the b-value drops exceed 10% below background level and examine whether eruptions occur within 10 days.We found that although most eruptions were preceded by days, months, or even years of escalating seismic activity, some eruptions occurred with little or no change in seismicity. On the other hand, of the 25 identified red lights, 40% are followed by eruption, whereas 60% are not. Among the latter, 71% involve red lights without subsequent eruptions but are mostly linked to large earthquakes, and 29% show no drop before the eruption. Our results are similar to those reported in studies using InSAR analysis, GNSS deformation, or thermal anomalies. This suggests that monitoring b-value changes is one of the most reliable indicators of impending eruptions. But, to better distinguish volcanic unrest from imminent eruptions, we recommend integrating b-value analysis with other geophysical observables and expert judgment.

presentations.presentation_title: Development and Preliminary Data Analysis of a New High-precision Terrestrial Magnetometer
presentations.abstract: Geomagnetic observation in Taiwan commenced in May 1965, followed by the immediate integration into the International Association of Geomagnetism and Aeronomy (IAGA). Initial observations focused on the hourly averages of magnetic declination, as well as horizontal and vertical components. Starting in 1979, the Institute of Earth Sciences, Academia Sinica (IESAS) established G826 total field magnetometers at Lunping (Taoyuan) and Tsengwen (Tainan) with a 5-minute sampling interval. In 1988, IESAS upgraded these to G856 proton precession magnetometers and expanded the network to eight continuous observation stations across Taiwan. In 2002, supported by the Ministry of Education’s Excellence Project for Earthquake Precursor Prediction, the network was further upgraded with Canadian-made GEM GSM90F magnetometers. With four additional stations, the sampling rate increased to one measurement every 5 seconds to calculate regional geomagnetic variations. Such data are critical for understanding geomagnetic behavior during quiet periods and monitoring intense fluctuations caused by magnetic storms, which can induce currents or electromagnetic pulses (EMP) affecting infrastructure. Furthermore, geomagnetic monitoring is instrumental in volcanic regions to observe changes in subsurface rock magnetization triggered by magma intrusion and volcanic activity. Presently, geomagnetic instruments used in Taiwan are primarily imported, posing challenges such as high costs, maintenance difficulties, and sampling rates (limited to 10 Hz) that are insufficient for high-precision research. To address these limitations, this study utilizes Ocean Bottom Electro-Magnetometer (OBEM) technology to develop a new high-precision terrestrial magnetometer, significantly increasing the sampling rate to 100 samples per second (100 Hz). In collaboration with Professor Cheng-Horng Lin of IESAS, this instrument is deployed to monitor magnetic field variations caused by magmatic activity in the Tatun Volcano Group. This thesis will discuss the instrument specifications, performance testing, field installation procedures, and preliminary data analysis.

presentations.presentation_title: RST Analysis of Underlying Conductivity Anomalies in Relation with Large Earthquakes in China from 2014 to 2022
presentations.abstract: Earthquakes are commonly considered to be processes of stress accumulation and release. Many studies have reported that the conductivity of underlying rocks can change during stress accumulations. In this study, subsurface conductivity changes associated with earthquakes (Ms >6) that occurred between 2014 and 2022 in China were investigated. The variations of the conductivity were examined utilizing Parkinson vectors derived from three-component geomagnetic data from over 100 permanent stations. Maps of daily spatial conductivity changes were constructed. To analyze the relationship between the conductivity changes and earthquakes, the Robust Satellite Techniques (RST) data analysis methodology was applied, for the first time, to define the potential Significant Sequence of Conductivity Anomalies (SSCAs) over nine years. The results reveal that all SSCAs were detected within approximately 1500 km of the epicenters, in the temporal range of 120 days before and after earthquakes occurrence. Significant enhancements were observed approximately from 95 to 15 days prior to the events. Furthermore, the high-conductivity areas were found to gradually migrate toward the epicenters over time, suggesting stress transfer from distant regions to near epicenter before earthquakes. The results show that in 73% of cases SCCAs occurred within 120 days before, and in the 27% of cases, within 120 days after earthquakes occurrence. These results suggest that SSCAs are more frequently observed prior to earthquakes than after them. This preliminary study highlights the potential of large-scale conductivity monitoring as an effective approach for understanding the earthquake preparation process.
presentations.session_title: Natural Hazards and Their Multi-sphere Coupling: from the Lithosphere to Space

presentations.presentation_title: Ionospheric and Plasmaspheric Electron Density Response from Geomagnetic Storm
presentations.abstract: With the widespread use of space technologies such as satellite communications and Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) in daily life, the impact of severe space weather on human activities has become increasingly significant. A focus of contemporary research is understanding how intense geomagnetic storms affect the ionosphere and plasmasphere, leading to dramatic transformations in plasma structures. However, studies of ionospheric variations during geomagnetic storms are often hindered by insufficient data, limited dimensions, or temporal discontinuities. For the plasmasphere, observational data are even sparser in both time and space, making research in this region particularly challenging. This study reconstructs the three-dimensional (3D) electron density structures of the ionosphere and plasmasphere under varying degrees of geomagnetic disturbance using data assimilation techniques. This approach integrates ground-based GNSS Total Electron Content (TEC) data with space-based absolute TEC data from the FORMOSAT-7/COSMIC-2 mission. The resulting continuous 3D electron density products will not only facilitate the study of 3D plasma evolution during geomagnetic storms but also enable direct investigation of coupling mechanisms between the ionosphere and plasmasphere. A deeper understanding of these 3D coupling processes can enhance predictive accuracy during geomagnetic storms and significantly contribute to severe space weather warning systems.
presentations.session_title: Natural Hazards and Their Multi-sphere Coupling: from the Lithosphere to Space

presentations.presentation_title: Source Tracing of Landslide Disaster Through Three-dimensional HF Doppler Sounding Array
presentations.abstract: Natural hazards excite acoustic and gravity waves that propagate upward, inducing detectable frequency shifts in the ionosphere. The High-Frequency (HF) Doppler sounder serves as a sensitive instrument for detecting these vertical ionospheric disturbances. Previous studies typically focus on ionospheric disturbances at a limited number of scattered altitudes, constraining the monitoring capability of Doppler array in three-dimensional space. This study utilizes an HF Doppler array comprising three frequency transmitters and five corresponding, receivers covering range of 200 to 300 km, to routinely monitor ionospheric layers between 200 and 250 km in altitudes. By integrating frequency shift observations from multiple HF Doppler instruments deployed at different altitudes and spatial locations, a spatial-temporal grid search algorithm is proposed that employs time-delay estimation and signal superposition techniques to enable real-time scanning of disturbances in three-dimensional space and inversion of natural hazard source locations. We selected the Doppler data from the period of the historical landslide for verification, and found that the source located by proposed method is basically consistent with the actual events. These results indicate that source tracing based on HF Doppler array is an effective technique and holds significant potential for the rapid detection of natural hazards.

presentations.presentation_title: Imminent Ionospheric Precursory Signatures Associated with Major Seismic Events in Japan
presentations.abstract: This paper investigates ionospheric precursory signatures for major earthquakes in Japan, specifically focusing on the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake (M7.6) and the 2025 Aomori earthquake (M7.5). The University of Electro-Communications (UEC) operates an extensive electromagnetic observation suite, utilizing a dense VLF/LF transmitter signal network to monitor perturbations in the lower ionosphere (D and E regions). Our analysis identifies distinct anomalies occurring a few hours prior to the onset of these seismic events, characterized by clear oscillations in the VLF/LF amplitude with periods ranging from tens to hundreds of minutes. These perturbations strongly imply Lithosphere-Atmosphere-Ionosphere (LAI) coupling triggered by Internal Gravity Waves (IGWs). Furthermore, the simultaneous detection of these anomalies across multiple transmitter-receiver paths reveals the spatial extent/propagation of the anomalies. The presence of Atmospheric Electric Field (AEF) anomalies near the epicenters—exhibiting similar oscillation periods under fair-weather conditions—further validates the AGW-mediated LAI coupling hypothesis for imminent seismic precursors.

presentations.presentation_title: On Solar‐terrestrial Interactions: Correlation Between Intense Geomagnetic Storms and Global Strong Earthquakes
presentations.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Solar‐terrestrial interactions are a topic of considerable interest and attention. In this paper, we introduce a new method called shift neighborhood matching correlation (SNMC) to investigate the relationship between geomagnetic storms and earthquakes across various time lags. To assess the significance of the correlations, we employ random sampling series to replace one or both of the time series. Analyzing nearly a century of data, our results reveal an increased likelihood of earthquakes following geomagnetic storms, particularly 27–28 days afterward. Conventional statistical methods confirm the significance of this correlation. However, when earthquakes are replaced with random series, the statistical significance derived from the SNMC method diminishes, highlighting the intrinsic properties of geomagnetic storm phenomena. We discuss two potential physical mechanisms to explain the correlations. While the earthquake probability gains solely based on geomagnetic storms is insufficient for reliable prediction, it may be useful in the integrated multi‐geophysical predictive models.

presentations.presentation_title: Exploring Extreme Space Weather and Atmosphere Interactions Through Surface Cosmogenic Radiosulfur Measurements
presentations.institution: Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Cosmogenic radiosulfur (sulfur-35) is produced in the atmosphere by high-energy particle interactions and serves as a sensitive tracer of stratospheric intrusions and solar activity. Our previous long-term measurements show that surface sulfur-35 concentrations are modulated by the 11-year solar cycle. Here, we report daily sulfur-35 measurements in surface air during May 2024, coinciding with an extreme solar storm (the “Mother’s Day” solar storm). We identify persistently elevated sulfur-35 levels during 9–15 May that occurred in the absence of stratospheric influence and coincided with enhanced solar energetic particle fluxes. These observations suggest that extreme solar storms may contribute to transient increases in atmospheric sulfur-35. Further researches on how other cosmogenic radionuclides respond to extreme space weather could deepen our understanding of past solar storms, aiding predictions of their future intensity, frequency, and potential impacts on spacecraft, radio communications, and even humans and ecosystems.

presentations.presentation_title: Impacts of Compound Hot-dry Events on Renewable Power in China Based on High-resolution Climate Projections
presentations.institution: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Compound hot-dry events (CHDE), characterized by simultaneous extreme heat and precipitation deficits, pose a dual threat to power systems by amplifying electricity demand while suppressing renewable generation capacity. Recent blackouts in China underscore the urgency of integrating such climate risks into energy planning. However, existing climate-energy modeling approaches rely on global climate outputs at resolutions too coarse to capture localized patterns and resource availability, often paired with empirical load and generation models that omit key operational constraints. As China accelerates its renewable energy transition, bridging this gap between climate science and power system modeling becomes increasingly critical, yet the value of high-resolution climate information for energy applications remains underexamined. This study investigates how climate change-induced CHDE affects power generation and demand in China, focusing particularly on the value of high-resolution climate data for energy planning. We first validate a Generative Adversarial Network-based downscaling model by reproducing the 2022 blackout events. We then downscale climate projections from three global models (GFDL-CM4, MPI-ESM1-2-HR, HadGEM3-GC31-MM) under SSP2-4.5 and SSP3-7.0 scenarios to 4-km, hourly resolution for the near-term (2041–2060) and long-term (2081–2100) periods. Using these downscaled outputs, we estimate renewable power generation potential and temperature-driven electricity demand, then conduct least-cost capacity expansion optimizations incorporating solar, wind, and hydropower resources. By comparing system configurations derived from coarse versus fine-resolution climate inputs, we quantify differences in planned capacity, system costs, and resource adequacy, and further assess uncertainties arising from emission scenarios, climate model selection, and system configurations. Our findings demonstrate that climate data resolution significantly influences energy system planning outcomes and that systematic uncertainty quantification across the modeling chain is essential for robust infrastructure investment decisions. [Acknowledgement] This research was supported by Research Grants Council of Hong Kong through Theme-based Research Scheme (T31-603/21-N) and General Research Fund (GRF16308722).
presentations.session_title: Observation, Modeling, and Assessment for Renewable Energy Sustainability

presentations.presentation_title: Climate-driven VRE Drought: Methods, Evidence, and Implications for Energy Systems
presentations.abstract: Climate change is increasing the variability of renewable energy production, raising concerns about prolonged periods of low output, commonly referred to as variable renewable energy (VRE) drought. A rapidly growing body of literature has examined VRE drought across different regions, technologies, and analytical approaches. However, differences in metrics, event definitions, and spatial and temporal scales make it challenging to compare results and to interpret VRE drought consistently from a climate perspective. In this study, global research on VRE drought is synthesized by systematically organizing both methodologies and reported findings. Existing studies are reviewed in terms of how VRE drought has been quantified, including the choice of metrics, thresholds, analytical scales, and data sources. Key results on observed and projected characteristics of VRE drought are then summarized, including its frequency, persistence, and concurrent occurrence across solar and wind generation. Evidence on associated climate drivers is also reviewed to provide a coherent climate context for these findings. By consolidating diverse approaches and results, this synthesis provides a structured reference for interpreting VRE drought as a climate-driven phenomenon and supports future studies that aim to link renewable energy production variability with climate mechanisms and energy system risk assessments.
presentations.session_title: Observation, Modeling, and Assessment for Renewable Energy Sustainability

presentations.presentation_title: Wind Power Potential Over South Korea Considering Wind Shear Coefficient Variability
presentations.abstract: Accurate assessment of wind power potential over South Korea requires reliable characterization of near-surface wind resources and their vertical extrapolation to turbine hub heights. While wind power potential is often estimated using reanalysis products and a fixed wind shear coefficient, the wind shear coefficient can vary substantially with atmospheric stability, surface roughness, season, and synoptic regimes, potentially biasing capacity factor estimates. In this study, we quantify observation-based wind power potential over South Korea by explicitly considering spatial and temporal variability in the wind shear coefficient.We use long-term in situ wind observations from the Korea Meteorological Administration to estimate wind speed at multiple heights and derive the wind shear coefficient via the power-law relationship. Hub-height wind speeds are reconstructed using both (i) a conventional fixed α approach and (ii) an observation-derived, time-varying α approach. Wind power potential is then evaluated using turbine power curves to compute capacity factor (CF) and related metrics, focusing on diurnal, seasonal, and interannual variability. Our results provide an observation-constrained baseline for wind power potential over South Korea and demonstrate that incorporating wind shear variability improves the realism of hub-height wind and CF estimates. The findings highlight the importance of wind shear characterization for robust wind resource assessment and for reducing uncertainty in climate-driven variability analyses and future projections.

presentations.presentation_title: Urban-Scale Parking Lot Mapping at Individual Space Level Using Google Earth Imagery and Deep Learning for Solar Panel Installation Planning
presentations.abstract: Parking lot solar photovoltaic systems have gained attention as a promising solution for carbon neutrality, with France mandating panel installation in large-scale parking lots by 2028. In Japan, while the government has established subsidy programs to support deployment, the lack of detailed parking lot datasets has hindered potential assessment and site selection studies. Existing datasets define parking lots as “parking spaces + driveways,” making it difficult to accurately estimate the installable area for solar panels. This study developed an automated method to extract parking spaces at the individual space level across urban scales using Google Earth imagery (20 cm resolution) and U-net deep learning architecture. We re-annotated 1,900 training images from Japan’s Geospatial Information Authority dataset with a refined definition: “parking spaces only” (clearly visible with white lines), excluding bus parking areas, driveways, and vehicle storage facilities with more than three rows. The trained model successfully processed the entire Urayasu City in 32 minutes, compared to an estimated 90 hours required for manual digitization. Validation in Kisarazu City demonstrated successful extraction at the parking space level, appropriately excluding driveways and bus parking areas. The model achieved an F1 score of 0.7251, with high Precision and moderate Recall, indicating strict control of false positives. Parking lot coverage rates varied significantly across study cities: Urayasu (5.72%), Kisarazu (1.50%), and Kamogawa (0.17%). This methodology enables city-scale assessment of solar panel installation potential and contributes to evidence-based planning for renewable energy deployment in urban areas.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​
presentations.session_title: Observation, Modeling, and Assessment for Renewable Energy Sustainability

presentations.presentation_title: Shifts in Surface Solar Radiation Across China Based on Gridded Data
presentations.abstract: China’s transition toward carbon neutrality relies heavily on photovoltaic (PV) expansion, yet the long-term stability of the solar resource—Downwards Surface Solar Radiation (DSSR)—remains uncertain due to complex atmospheric interactions. This study provides a comprehensive assessment of DSSR spatiotemporal variability across China to guide renewable energy planning. Using ERA5-Land reanalysis data validated against ground observations, we applied a novel time–length triangle framework and SHAP-based machine learning interpretation to decouple trend non-stationarity from atmospheric drivers. We identify distinct temporal phases: a "dimming" era, a "brightening" period, and a recent reversal to decline. A critical spatial divergence was observed: high-potential regions like the Tibetan Plateau and Western China are experiencing significant radiation decreases, whereas lower-radiation demand centers in the North and South show slight increases. Attribution analysis reveals that water vapor and cloud cover are the primary regulators of DSSR, with aerosols exerting notable negative forcing in industrialized Eastern and Central regions. These findings expose a growing spatial mismatch between solar resource availability and energy demand. To address this, we advocate for enhanced west-to-east power transmission infrastructure and multi-energy complementary systems, alongside strict emission controls to mitigate aerosol-induced solar dimming.
presentations.session_title: Observation, Modeling, and Assessment for Renewable Energy Sustainability

presentations.presentation_title: Implementation Gap in Global Power Capacity Expansion to Meet Paris Agreement Climate Targets
presentations.abstract: Meeting the Paris Agreement’s climate targets demands an unprecedented expansion of renewable energy. Despite global commitments, significant implementation gaps persist due to economic, policy, and technical uncertainties. Here, we develop a Global Power Capacity Dynamics Framework, integrating facility-level data, machine learning and transition modelling to assess the feasibility of global power expansion. Analyzing 215,849 power plant units across five status modes (operating, planned, cancelled, standby, retired), the framework explicitly incorporates the likelihood of planned capacity realization and the conversion of existing fossil assets. We find that by 2030, only 51% [40–61%] of announced planned capacity is expected to become operational, while 26% [19–36%] is likely to be cancelled, with fossil fuel projects, especially coal, facing a cancellation rate of about 35%. Global operational capacity is projected to reach 9,727 GW [9,626–9,848], including 178 GW [159–198] of existing fossil units requiring conversion or replacement (e.g., coal-to-gas, fossil-to-biomass). Although renewables dominate the planned pipeline, they are projected to constitute only 52% of the global energy mix by 2030, well below levels needed to meet climate goals. Regional disparities are pronounced: Asia, despite its relatively low cancellation rate, faces the world’s largest implementation gap, requiring an additional 2,488 GW of solar and contending with 523 GW of stranded coal capacity to remain on a 1.5 °C pathway. This study provides the first probabilistic, facility-level assessment of global power capacity trajectories, revealing critical shortfalls in planned deployment and underscoring the urgency of aligning capacity expansion with climate targets.
presentations.session_title: Observation, Modeling, and Assessment for Renewable Energy Sustainability

presentations.presentation_title: An Educational Board Game for Net-zero Transition: Design and Effectiveness
presentations.abstract: This research aims to develop a game-based system to cultivate competencies aligned with the Net-Zero Transition (NZT), thereby enhancing students’ issue literacy and promoting positive behavioral intentions. The integrated system combines a physical board game with a digital system. The board game encompasses the Energy, Industry, Lifestyle, and Society Transitions inherent to the NZT framework. Players assume the roles of six distinct stakeholders: Government, Scientific Research Institution, Manufacturer, Merchant, Associations, and the Public. By deploying their organization-specific cards, players collaboratively confront the impacts of climate change while striving to achieve net-zero emissions. The digital system facilitates the calculation of complex interrelationships between critical factors, including electricity, carbon emissions, population, manpower, and economic performance. Focusing on the Energy Transition theme, we developed the Transition Knowledge and Creative Problem-Solving questionnaires, to analyze outcomes across environmental, economic, and social dimensions. We also developed the Transition Attitude Scale and the Game Usage Experience Scale. Results from a sample of undergraduate students indicate that learners exhibited heightened awareness of the reliance of net-zero emission transition methods on economic and social factors. They further recognized that economic and societal factors are crucial elements in inter-organizational interactions concerning sustainability issues. In Creative Problem-Solving performance, post-test scores for the environment and social themes were significantly higher than pre-test scores, although the economic theme showed no significant difference. In the Transition Attitude post-test, students demonstrated a greater recognition of the importance of the Energy Transition, and their behavioral intentions also increased. The game experience primarily focused on organizational interaction and the strategic conceptualization of collaborative actions.
presentations.session_title: General Session

presentations.presentation_title: Integrating Operational Space Weather Monitoring and Secondary Education Outreach in Taiwan
presentations.abstract: In alignment with Taiwan’s rapid advancements in scientific sounding rockets and satellites, there is a growing necessity to integrate space weather awareness into formal education. While the Central Weather Administration (CWA) has established a foundation for space-related public outreach and operational monitoring since 2015, the current challenge lies in integrating these specialized fields into formal education. This study focuses on the development of a comprehensive 18-week elective course designed to broaden high school students' understanding of the space domain. The curriculum moves beyond traditional classroom learning by covering a diverse range of topics, including space environment, remote sensing, satellite missions, and rocketry. To ensure a practical understanding of space technology, the program incorporates hands-on projects using satellite data, CubeSat assembly activities, and field trips to space exhibitions and operational facilities. The primary goal of this initiative is to equip students with the scientific literacy needed to navigate the complexities of modern space-based society. Furthermore, the course aims to provide a standardized set of teaching resources and lesson plans for Earth science educators across the country. By prioritizing a broad-based education in space science and technology, this program directly supports the strategic goals of Taiwan’s Space Science White Paper and ensures workforce readiness for future national space endeavors.
presentations.session_title: General Session

presentations.presentation_title: Meeting the Moment: Sustaining Climate Science and Engagement in Shifting Policy Environments
presentations.abstract: Rapid shifts in U.S. climate policy have introduced uncertainty around the continuity of national assessments and participation in international scientific processes, raising concerns about maintaining the evidence-base for informed decision-making. This presentation examines how scientific societies, research institutions, and individual researchers are coordinating across disciplinary and national boundaries to safeguard the integrity and accessibility of climate science during periods of geopolitical and policy volatility. It will highlight collaborative strategies that reinforce resilience across the climate enterprise. These include a new cross-society journal access initiative led by AGU and the American Meteorological Society, designed to ensure uninterrupted global access to peer-reviewed climate research. The presentation also explores coordinated nomination pathways and access agreements that enable U.S. -based scientists to continue contributing to international assessment processes, such as IPCC’s Seventh Assessment Report, despite shifting domestic policy priorities. Beyond these examples, the presentation situates these efforts within a broader framework of institutional coordination and transnational scientific networks. By leveraging partnerships across disciplinary and national boundaries, the research community is developing adaptive mechanisms to sustain engagement, preserve scientific continuity, and uphold the principles of open science. These practical models offer a roadmap for global research communities navigating similar disruptions, underscoring the critical role of scientific societies in bridging gaps between research, policy and international engagement.
presentations.session_title: General Session

presentations.presentation_title: Online Stargazing in Times of Disruption
presentations.institution: University of the Philippines National Institute for Science and Mathematics Education Development
presentations.abstract: The University of the Philippines National Institute for Science and Mathematics Education Development (UP NISMED) regularly conducts stargazing sessions for schools to augment the teaching and learning of Earth and Space Science in the basic education curriculum in the Philippines through its stargazing program. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020, all mass gathering events were prohibited, affecting the conduct of in-person stargazing sessions. In December 2020, a rare conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn occurred. With the intention of sharing the event with teachers, students, and the general public, the institute’s High School Earth Science Group decided to bring the stargazing session online. Subsequent sessions featured live and detailed instructions given to online participants. Participants interacted with the online facilitators, allowing them to locate and view night sky objects independently from their own homes. Since its initial success, the institute has produced over 20 online stargazing and astronomy education webinars on Earth and Space Science learning competencies across grade levels. This has inspired educators to adopt and utilize the curriculum materials discussed in the sessions. The online format has enabled the institute to reach a wider audience than normally possible before the pandemic. This initiative marked the first implementation of an online stargazing format. When similar disruptions occur in the future, the online format may again be utilized to ensure the continued delivery of astronomy education. In 2025, the UP NISMED Stargazing Program was awarded the University of the Philippines Diliman’s Gawad Tsanselor para sa Natatanging Programang Pang-Ekstensyon.
presentations.session_title: General Session

presentations.presentation_title: Telescope Workshop for Educators
presentations.institution: University of the Philippines National Institute for Science and Mathematics Education Development
presentations.abstract: The Department of Education (DepEd) tapped the University of the Philippines National Institute for Science and Mathematics Education Development (UP NISMED) to recommend specifications of telescopes that would be procured and issued to public schools. In 2020, these telescopes were distributed but remained unutilized because teachers lacked the necessary knowledge and skills to operate them. Training in telescope use could have addressed this challenge but was not possible due to the COVID-19 pandemic. When schools returned to face-to-face classes, the UP NISMED High School Earth Science Group developed and conducted a telescope workshop for teachers from schools that received DepEd-issued telescopes. The workshop was designed to address persistent gaps in astronomy instruction in basic education, where teaching is constrained by limited experience in observing sky objects and celestial phenomena. As this was the first time that such a workshop was conducted, several challenges emerged. Teachers were unfamiliar with telescopes, resulting in situations such as the disassembly of the main optical mirror, the telescope pointing toward the ground, and the cover not being removed. These experiences underscored the need for a less theoretical and more hands-on approach. The workshop was then refined to emphasize the basic parts, assembly, and proper usage of telescopes. After the training, some teachers conducted their own telescope workshops and observation activities in their respective schools. These activities were intended to support students’ engagement in practical astronomy and the learning of basic astronomy concepts related to the Moon, planets, and other observable objects in the Solar System. To provide sustained assistance, an online support group was established to offer guidance related to telescope use. Having initially served schools mostly in Metro Manila, the program aims to expand its reach by conducting workshops in other regions of the country.

presentations.presentation_title: Feasibility of Trans-himalayan Region Tsokar as an Analogue Space Station to Study Hypoxic Adaptations in Analogue Astronauts
presentations.abstract: Space stations operate under partial cabin depressurization to reduce the risk of decompression sickness during frequent extravehicular activities, but this increases the likelihood of chronic mild hypoxia in astronauts. Detecting physiological adaptation to hypoxia is therefore critical for astronaut health and for terrestrial analogue studies. High-altitude environments offer a natural setting to investigate hypoxic responses under realistic operational constraints.This study evaluates the feasibility of the trans-Himalayan region of Tsokar, Ladakh, as an analogue space station environment for studying physiological adaptation to hypoxia. Two analogue astronauts participated in a ten-day isolation mission at the Himalayan Outpost for Planetary Exploration (HOPE), a two-module analogue habitat located at 4530 m above sea level. Participants performed controlled stress-inducing experiments in isolation. Multimodal physiological signals—photoplethysmography (PPG), electrocardiography (ECG), and electrodermal activity (EDA)—were recorded using wearable sensors (CardioBAN, PLUX Biosignals, Portugal, and Biopac Ring, BIOPAC Systems, USA). Data were compared against baseline recordings obtained at low altitude (Delhi, 300 m) and moderate high altitude (Leh, 3500 m).Physiological features derived from EDA, PPG, and ECG were analyzed to assess altitude-dependent differences and temporal adaptations over the mission. Effect sizes were quantified using Cliff’s Delta and Cohen’s d. Skin conductance response rates increased initially and subsequently adapted toward low-altitude baseline levels (δ ≈ 0.07). ECG-derived heart rate variability metrics showed a pronounced early reduction in mean peak-to-peak intervals (δ = 0.78), followed by partial adaptation later in the mission (δ = 0.53). Consistent physiological changes associated with hypoxic exposure were observed across the isolation period. Differences between ECG- and PPG-derived HRV metrics further highlight the importance of multimodal wearable sensing.These findings demonstrate that Tsokar elicits measurable hypoxic adaptations, supporting its suitability as an analogue site for hypoxia-related studies relevant to future human space missions.

presentations.presentation_title: A Facet of Japanʼs and International Trends of Open Science and Research Data Policies and Promotions
presentations.abstract: Open Science (OS), or the potential game change of the scholarly research ecosystem, has been emerging issues for past years. The author’s decadal efforts and experience are introduced, of helping national/international OS policy making and engaging a few research communities, and related works with science stakeholders and researchers. The author has been continuously working with G7 Open Science WG (co-chair countries of EU and Japan) since its establishment at G7 Science Ministers’ Meeting 2016 under the Japanese presidency, currently working as a WG co-chair. In contrast to such high-level OS policy making with guiding Japan’s national OS policy, also his experience includes close communications with the earth and planetary science researcher community. He has been trying to encourage scientists of Japan Geoscience Union (JpGU; ~10k members) to lookat and recognize importance of OS, in partnership with American Geophysical Union (AGU; ~60k members) and European Geosciences Union (EGU; ~16,000 members). There needed a decade that influential scientists in JpGU started to touch and work on OS and FAIR data issues gradually and increasingly in the last couple of years. Knowing how the scientists handle and faces efforts, barriers and incentives of research data management, metadata, persistent identifiers (such as DOI etc.), the top-down and bottom-up approaches have been proceeding in parallel. It is important to recognize how the real scientists are working for immediate Open Access publishing and research data sharing aligned to the OS and FAIR principles, which should be incorporated into national and international policies, principles and guidelines. The Change of Research Culture or community norm is the gist of our challenges to make the benefit of Open Science reality.
presentations.session_title: General Session

presentations.presentation_title: Mid-Holocene Paleoenvironment of Matsu Area Inferred from Stable Isotope Compositions of Chipinglong Archaeological Gastropod Shells
presentations.abstract: We have analyzed stable isotope records of 14 archaeological Reishia shells collected from Chipinglong archaeological sites (~4500-4000 yrBP), 6 modern Reishia shells, and 76 water samples collected from Dongiu and Nangan Islands, to reconstruct the Mid-Holocene paleoenvironment of Matsu area.Mean hydrogen and oxygen isotope values of water samples are respectively -2.2 ± 2.5‰ (mean ± 1σ; N = 74; V-SMOW) and -0.8 ± 0.3‰ for Nangan; -1.7 ± 1.6‰ (N = 2) and -0.8 ± 0.2‰ for Dongju. There is no significant difference in isotope values and salinity observed between Nangan and Dongiu water. The water oxygen isotope values show the seasonal fluctuation and is related to the amount of freshwater mixed with the seawater.Mean oxygen isotope value of the Reishia shells from the Chipinglong Site is -1.6 ± 0.5‰ (N = 1484；V-PDB) and is comparable to that of modern Reishia shells (-1.6 ± 0.6‰; N=352). It indicates that the average seawater temperature in 4500 to 4000 years B.P. may be comparable to that of modern seawater. However, the minimum oxygen isotope value of the archaeological Reishia shells is less than that of modern Reishia shells, indicating possible more freshwater input to the Matsu area due to the heavier rainfalls on south east region of China in 4500 to 4000 years B.P. Seasonal fluctuations in oxygen isotope values were observed in both modern and archaeological specimens. The harvest seasons for Chipinglong Reishia shells were mainly in summer and autumn (spring, N=2；summer, N=4；autumn, N=5).The average carbon isotope value of the Chipinglong archaeological Reishia shells (1.1 ± 0.6‰) is about 1.7‰ greater than that of the modern Reishia shells (-0.6 ± 0.9‰), indicating that the primary productivity of Matsu area in 4,500 to 4,000 years B.P. was higher than that of present.

presentations.presentation_title: The Role of the Temperature Dependence of Cloud Phase in Simulating the Arctic Climate During the Last Interglacial
presentations.abstract: The Last Interglacial (LIG), approximately 129,000 to 116,000 years ago, was a relatively warm period, during which the global mean temperature is estimated to have been about 0.5–1.5 °C higher than in the preindustrial period. Differences in Earth’s orbital parameters led to particularly warm conditions in the Arctic, and it has been suggested that summer sea ice may have disappeared. In the previous study, a positive correlation was demonstrated across climate models between summer sea-ice area during the Last Interglacial and that under increased CO₂ conditions expected for the future, implying that the skill of simulating LIG sea ice is linked to the reliability of future projections. In this study, we investigate how the temperature dependence used in climate models to determine cloud phase—that is, the fraction of cloud particles in liquid versus solid form—affects the reproduction of Arctic climate during the Last Interglacial. Using the MIROC4mV and MIROC4m models, we conducted numerical experiments with and without dynamic vegetation feedback, as well as experiments in which the temperature dependence of the liquid fraction of cloud particles was varied. The results differ substantially depending on the presence or absence of vegetation feedback associated with albedo feedback and on the representation of cloud phase related to the winter greenhouse effect, demonstrating the importance of both factors in simulating the Arctic climate during the Last Interglacial. (This abstract is based on preprint, https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2025-4109)

presentations.presentation_title: Abrupt Hydroclimatic Changes During the Last Deglaciation Inferred from Varved Sediment Composition of Lake Suigetsu, Japan
presentations.institution: The University of Tokyo, Faculty of Science
presentations.abstract: Abrupt and non-linear climate responses are a key feature of the last deglaciation (~16-10 ka), when the climate system repeatedly shifted between distinct modes, including the Bølling–Allerød (B–A) warming. Lake Suigetsu (central Japan) preserves annually laminated sediments with a robust varve-based chronology tied to terrestrial radiocarbon anchors, providing a unique archive for sub-decadal paleoclimate reconstructions. Following an abrupt warming recorded in pollen assemblages at Lake Suigetsu that preceded Greenland by ~200 years, a ~200-year interval marked by frequent flood events—the Stormy Two Centuries (STC)—has been linked to a threshold-like reorganization of the Asian westerly jet, yet associated hydroclimatic and dust-transport changes remain poorly constrained. This study conducted centimeter-scale (~10-year resolution) analyses of biogenic silica (BSi) content and flux to evaluate hydroclimate variability in the last deglaciation. BSi content was quantified using alkaline extraction, with dissolved Si and Al measured by ICP–AES. To calculate fluxes, we also measured dry bulk density at 1 cm intervals continuously. The result shows that increases in BSi wt% and flux precede the B/A abrupt warming in Greenland. Our results support the pollen-derived abrupt warming and suggest earlier limnological response to hydroclimatic forcing that preceded terrestrial vegetation changes. The reconstructions provide new constraints on the timing and mechanisms of hydroclimate change during the last deglaciation.
