presentations.presentation_title: Coupled Carbon-cycle Perturbations and Sea-level Change in the Early Triassic Recorded in an Oceanic-plate Seamount Carbonate Succession
presentations.abstract: Following the Smithian Thermal Maximum (STM) of the Olenekian (Early Triassic), climate shifted abruptly to cooler conditions across the Smithian–Spathian boundary (SSB) amid pronounced carbon-cycle perturbations. We examine this transition in the Taho Formation (Taho Limestone) exposed in Seiyo City, Ehime Prefecture, Japan, using paired δ 13 C carb and δ 13 C org , total organic carbon (TOC), thin-section petrography, and biomarker distributions. Carbonate carbon isotopes reach a marked negative minimum during the STM and shift positively at the SSB. Thin sections indicate that late Smithian strata are dominated by storm-derived deposits, whereas the SSB interval contains numerous erosional surfaces, consistent with sea-level fall and repeated seafloor reworking; Spathian strata display intertidal fabrics, indicating progressive shallowing after the boundary. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons occur throughout the section, and coronene is most abundant near horizons with negative δ 13 C carb peaks, linking high-temperature heating events—most plausibly volcanism—to the STM isotope minimum. Across the SSB, TOC covaries positively with δ13Ccarb, suggesting enhanced primary productivity and organic-carbon burial contributed to the positive isotope shift and associated cooling. Sea-level decline during SSB cooling likely promoted seafloor erosion and formation of black intraclasts through reworking of organic-rich material. Deposited on an oceanic-plate seamount far from continental-margin subsidence patterns, the Taho Limestone provides a low-noise record in which the SSB sea-level fall and erosion can be linked directly to global cooling tied to carbon-cycle change.

presentations.presentation_title: Intensification of East Asian Winter Monsoon Since 400 Ka Reconstructed from a Set of the Japan Sea Sediment Cores
presentations.abstract: East Asian winter monsoon (EAWM) promotes the sea-ice expansion in the northern Japan Sea which could supply coarse clastic materials to the sediments. EAWM also makes the surface water density higher by cooling and brine ejection during the sea-ice formation, which leads to the strong ventilation of the deeper water column of the Japan Sea. Therefore, the preservation of organic matter and carbonate in the deeper part of the Japan Sea is considered to be controlled by the balance between the productivity promoted by summer nutrient input and the organic matter decomposition / carbonate dissolution by winter ventilation. IODP Exp. 346 in 2013 collected 7 mostly perfectly continuous sediment cores which could be correlated among others in millennial time scale utilizing cyclic deposition of dark and light color sediments formed by basin wide synchronous production-decomposition of organic matter (TOC). One of the core set, IODP Site U1422, is located in the northern Japan Sea, which enabled us to measured the contents of detrital sand as ice-rafted detritus (IRD) and mineral composition of the mud fraction using a powder X-ray diffraction analysis (XRD).IRD contents at Site U1422 are higher during glacial times and lower during interglacial times. The amplitude of IRD variability increases after 400 ka. Calcite content detected by XRD shows large variability before 400 ka, and significantly reduced after that. In association of these changes at 400 ka, organic carbon preservation became poorer after 400 ka compared to those before at all the site. These lines of evidence suggest that sea-ice expansion was more frequent after 400 ka, which was associated with the stronger ventilation of the deeper water column leading to enhanced decomposition of organic matter and dissolution of carbonate due to shallowed carbonate compensation depth, which could be the results of an intensified EAWM at that time.

presentations.presentation_title: Indo-Pacific Warm Pool Hydroclimate During Marine Isotope Stage 11 Inferred from Isotope-enabled Coupled Climate Simulations
presentations.institution: Faculty of Earth Sciences and Technology, Institut Teknologi Bandung
presentations.abstract: Tropical hydroclimate in the Pacific and Indian Oceans is tightly coupled to the Indo-Pacific Warm Pool (IPWP) sea surface temperature (SST), and its evolution remains uncertain under ongoing anthropogenic warming. Here, we investigate IPWP climate at the Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 11 peak (409 ka), considered as a potential analogue to the present interglacial. We use the global coupled isotope-enabled Community Earth System Model (iCESM1.2) with ~1° horizontal resolution and compare the results with pre-industrial (PI) conditions. Our results show warmer-than-PI annual mean SST up to 0.4°C in the western equatorial Pacific and Indian Ocean basins, while the eastern part of both basins shows cooling by up to 0.4°C at 409 ka, relative to PI. Precipitation anomalies are positive over the western Indian Ocean, the Asian continent, and Indonesia, with local maxima up to 1.6 mm/day, and negative over the eastern Indian Ocean and the central equatorial Pacific, reaching -0.8 mm/day. This suggests a La Niña-like state and positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) phase at 409 ka. Negative sea surface salinity (SSS) anomalies are controlled mostly by the influx of fresh water from the Asian continent and western Indonesia, as shown by the anomaly value reaching -1.2 psu in the north of Bengal Bay and western Indonesian waters, which is consistent with negative anomalies of surface δ 18 O sw . Meanwhile, positive SSS anomalies of up to 0.5 psu in the equatorial Pacific, are associated with lower precipitation and higher surface temperatures at 409 ka relative to PI. A higher-than-PI SSS simulated in the south of Indonesia could be attributed to enhanced upwelling during the positive IOD phase. For the ongoing analysis, we compare SST and δ 18 O sw reconstructions from various points in the IPWP region with simulations to further investigate local changes and model-proxy consistency.

presentations.presentation_title: VERTECS: Astronomical nano satellite to observe visible extragalactic background light
presentations.abstract: Visible Extragalactic background RadiaTion Exploration by CubeSat (VERTECS) is a 6U astronomical CubeSat to investigate the cosmic star formation history from the early universe to the present epoch through observations of the extragalactic background light (EBL) in the visible wavelength. Earlier observations have shown that the near-infrared EBL is several times brighter than integrated light of individual galaxies. As candidates for the excess light, first-generation stars in the early universe or low-redshift intra-halo light have been proposed. Since these objects are expected to show different emission spectra in visible wavelengths, multi-color visible observations are crucial to reveal the origin of the excess light. The VERTECS satellite is equipped with a 3U-sized wide-field telescope optimized for observation of the visible EBL. Since detection sensitivity of the EBL depends on the product of the telescope aperture and the field of view, it is possible to observe it with a small but wide-field telescope system that can be mounted on the limited volume of CubeSat. The bus system is based on heritage of series of CubeSats developed at Kyushu Institute of Technology. From the mission requirements, a high-precision attitude control unit, a high-speed X-band transmitter for image downlink, and deployable solar array paddle are integrated into the CubeSat bus system. VERTECS was selected for JAXA-Small Satellite Rush Program (JAXA-SMASH Program), a new program that encourages universities, private companies and JAXA to collaborate to realize small satellite missions utilizing commercial small launch opportunities, and to diversify transportation services in Japan. The satellite development started from 2022 and it is now in the final stage of flight model development, waiting for launch by the H3 Launch Vehicle.
presentations.session_title: Space Science and Education Using Nano/microsatellite(s)

presentations.presentation_title: Measurements of Deep Space Radiation Aboard the ispace Resilience Lunar Lander
presentations.abstract: Regions outside of Low Earth Orbit are classified as “deep space”. The deep space environment poses many challenges for human and robotic exploration, including stronger ionizing radiation fluxes, more extreme temperature variations, as well as limited data downlink volume. With the growth of flight opportunities to deep space aboard government and commercial lunar missions, characterizing the radiation environment and its effects on electronics during these missions is of critical importance for both crewed and uncrewed missions. We have completed the rapid development and deployment of a Deep Space Radiation Probe (DSRP), which was launched aboard the HAKUTO-R Mission 2 Resilience lunar lander from Commercial Lunar Payload Services provider ispace, inc. on January 15, 2025, immediately commencing operations following launch. Mounted on the exterior of the lander with minimal shielding, DSRP measured the radiation dose, dose rate, and single event upset rate throughout the five-month mission, including multiple passes through the radiation belts, at distances far beyond the Moon, as well as in lunar orbit, being active for over 97% of the five-month mission. The largest measured radiation dose rates are considerably larger than those aboard past lunar missions during lower solar activity levels. Passage through the radiation belts and solar radiation storms were correlated with increases in dose rate, while bit flips caused by single event upsets that can result in data corruption and flight software malfunction were detected throughout the course of mission, not solely during events where higher particle radiation fluxes are expected such as solar radiation storms. A steady background deep space dose rate was also observed during quiet times due to galactic cosmic rays. The radiation data provided by DSRP with its unusually long mission duration will be beneficial for the development of future spacecraft electronics and crewed missions to deep space and the Moon.

presentations.presentation_title: Equatorial Sentinels for Environment: a Tandem Microwave Radiometer and Hyperspectral Cubesat Mission Design for Environmental Science Around the Tropics
presentations.abstract: South East Asian countries require high-frequency, high-resolution Earth observation data to address fast-changing environmental, agricultural, and urban challenges. This paper presents a concept study for a dual-satellite, low-cost mission consisting of: A passive microwave radiometer microsatellite providing all-weather, cloud-penetrating observations of soil moisture, rainfall proxies, and thermal anomalies; and A hyperspectral CubeSat optimized for fine-resolution land and maritime surface characterization. Both satellites operate in coordinated Near-Equatorial Orbits (less than 15° inclination) to maximize revisit over Singapore and the equatorial belt.The study investigates mission objectives and system-level requirements for both CubeSats. It focuses on the synergistic benefits of integrating passive microwave and hyperspectral measurements in a coordinated train. Areas of study include: Intelligence transfer between CubeSats; Ocean, water quality and atmosphere monitoring; Increased data yield under frequent tropical cloud cover; Cross-calibration opportunities between optical and microwave channels; and Reduced mission cost; as well as unique geopolitical collaboration frameworks. This dual-satellite mission presents a new revolution in remote sensing by proposing simple, lower-cost sensors that complement and enhance existing systems, offering a transformative and scalable pathway for high-frequency environmental intelligent monitoring across the Tropical belt.

presentations.presentation_title: Solar-cycle-aware Orbital Lifetime Modeling for ISS-deployed 1U Cubesats Using Weibull–gaussian Processes
presentations.abstract: The orbital lifetime of 1U CubeSats deployed from the International Space Station (ISS) is strongly modulated by thermospheric density variations driven by geomagnetic disturbances and solar cycle activity. In this study, orbital lifetime is formally defined as the elapsed time from ISS deployment to atmospheric re-entry (approximately 150 km altitude) and represented as a continuous orbital lifetime function describing altitude decay over time. Using observational data from 23 CubeSats released between 2012 and 2024, we model orbital decay with a Weibull cumulative distribution function, which effectively captures the accelerated and nonlinear nature of altitude loss. The Weibull-based formulation achieves a high coefficient of determination in reconstructing orbital trajectories (R² ≈ 0.99). To incorporate solar-driven variability, Weibull parameters are estimated through Gaussian Process Regression using the F10.7 solar activity index, deployment altitude, and a normalized solar cycle phase as explanatory variables. The resulting model reproduces observed lifetime functions with R² > 0.8 and predicts re-entry timing with an uncertainty of approximately 0.5–2 months. The primary contribution of this work is the adaptation of Weibull lifetime modeling—originally developed in reliability engineering—to satellite orbital decay analysis, enabling compact and physically interpretable representation of lifetime evolution with a limited number of parameters. Furthermore, the inclusion of normalized solar cycle phase enhances predictive performance beyond conventional activity indices by implicitly encoding phase-dependent solar wind structures. This framework provides a robust and efficient tool for estimating CubeSat orbital lifetimes under varying solar cycle conditions.

presentations.presentation_title: On-orbit Flight Results and Lessons Learned from the SPATIUM-II Mission
presentations.abstract: KITSUNE/SPATIUM-II was developed as a dual-satellite system housed within a single structure, with both satellites successfully operated in low-Earth orbit for approximately one year, from March 2022 to March 2023. SPATIUM-II represents the second mission of the SPATIUM program and was developed through a collaboration between the Kyushu Institute of Technology and Nanyang Technological University. The SPATIUM program aims to demonstrate key technologies required for three-dimensional ionospheric mapping using a chip-scale atomic clock (CSAC), prior to achieving scientific-level total electron content (TEC) measurements. The SPATIUM-II payload received a spread-spectrum BPSK signal at 450 MHz transmitted from a ground station, which was demodulated and processed onboard to estimate the signal propagation time delay between the ground station and the satellite. A CSAC was employed as the clock source for the receiver software-defined radio, while a 1-PPS signal from the onboard GPS receiver was used to achieve time synchronization between the ground system and the satellite receiver. In addition, the secondary mission was a store-and-forward mission through LoRa receivers from the ground sensor terminals in multiple developing countries and Japan. This study presents lessons learned from the on-orbit TEC technology demonstration, based on flight results, and discusses potential improvements for future small-satellite missions targeting precise ionospheric TEC measurements as well as store-and-forward missions.

presentations.presentation_title: Insights on Leading a Student Team for Taiwan's Largest Cubesat Mission: Scion-x
presentations.abstract: SCIntillation and IONosphere eXtended (SCION-X) is a 12U CubeSat project initiated in 2019 through a "Space Mission Design" graduate course at National Central University (NCU), Taiwan. This CubeSat is scheduled for launch aboard SpaceX Transporter 17 by June 2026. SCION-X has 3 different science payloads and 1 service payload. There are 3 different RF modules in 3 distinct frequencies. The system becomes complicated and it is challenging for the system to coordinate and share resources among payloads and subsystems. Plus, the more payloads, means more constraints for the system according to different measurement requirements, which increase the complexity of the concept of operation and the spacecraft operation modes. The technical team is around 20 people, including PI, an assistant, a post-doc, graduate students, and undergraduate students. Conducting a satellite project requires more than just technical skills. The managing skill is the key to have the team moving in the correct direction. Furthermore, the involvement of stakeholders ensures the funding, deadlines, and specific technical support. Another one of the biggest challenges that every student team struggles, is the quality and quantity of students. Due to the nature of space projects, students are rarely able to go through the whole project life cycle, most of the time even the development phase. Space mission projects offer students more than just academic research opportunities. They provide invaluable practical engineering experience, cultivate problem-solving abilities, and foster teamwork skills essential for industry demands. This paper outlines key insights in managing a 20-person higher education team, technical development, and team cultivation in a complex satellite mission, and ensuring knowledge transfer for future generations of space engineers, highlighting key takeaways for developing robust student-led space initiatives.

presentations.presentation_title: Early In-orbit Observations and Data Processing of Iammap on Cas500-3
presentations.abstract: The Ionospheric Anomaly Monitoring by Magnetometer And Plasma-probe (IAMMAP) onboard the Compact Advanced Satellite CAS500-3 has been successfully operated during its early mission phase, since the successful launch on 27th November in 2025 by KSLV-III(Korean Space Launch Vehicle), providing initial in-orbit measurements of ionospheric plasma and magnetic field variations. This paper presents a newly developed data processing system based on a Network Database architecture, capable of real-time data registration and processing. It reports analysis results from early operational data obtained from the Langmuir Probe (LP), Impedance Probe (IP), and Adaptive In-phase Magnetometer (AIMAG), and defines the Level-0 and Level-1 data product structure and processing framework for IAMMAP observations. Early mission datasets enable observations of electron density and electron temperature associated with the equatorial ionization anomaly (EIA), as well as magnetic field perturbations related to the intensity of the equatorial electrojet (EEJ). These measurements demonstrate the potential for analyzing the complex relationships among major electrodynamic processes occurring in the equatorial ionosphere. In addition, the study discusses the expected data quality and scientific applicability of IAMMAP measurements during the nominal mission phase, based on findings from early operations.

presentations.presentation_title: Preliminary Results from Compact Ionospheric Probe Onboard Pearl-1a/1b CubeSat
presentations.abstract: PEARL-1A/1B (Propagation Experiment using kurz-Above-band radio in Low earth orbit) CubeSat conducted by National Central University (NCU) for educational training/scientific research were scheduled to launch into a sun-synchronous orbit at 590 km altitude around 1100 local time sector by SpaceX CAS500-2 rideshare mission from Vandenberg Space Force Base in 2026Q2. A Compact Ionospheric Probe (CIP) was installed onboard PEARL-1A/1B to monitor global ionospheric space weather conditions resulting in space communication disruption and navigation outage for a 3-years mission. The CIP is an all-in-one in-situ ion sensor also developed by NCU to measure ionospheric ion concentration, velocity, and temperature alternatively like its predecessor, Advanced Ionospheric Probe, onboard FORMOSAT-5 satellite. In this presentation, preliminary observations derived from the CIP measurements will be presented and some works on CubeSat operations will also be discussed in an in-orbit check phase.

presentations.presentation_title: The Pre-earthquake Ionospheric Anomalies and the Possible Coupling Mechanism Related to the M8.8 Kamchatka Earthquake Occurred on July 29, 2025
presentations.abstract: The pre-earthquake ionospheric anomalies (PEIAs) in the F2 layer prior to the M8.8 Kamchatka earthquake on July 29, 2025, in Russia were detected through both ground-based and space-borne observations. Multiple parameters were analyzed, including the total electron content (TEC) from Global Ionosphere Maps and Global Navigation Satellite System, F2 layer critical frequency (foF2) observed by ionosondes, electron density (Ne), and geomagnetic field components recorded by the Swarm satellite. After excluding the influences of geomagnetic and solar activities, anomalies in TEC, foF2, Ne and geomagnetic variations on July 20 and 21 within ~3600 km of the epicenter were identified as likely PEIAs. To explore the possible lithosphere-atmosphere-ionosphere coupling mechanism, we further examined three atmospheric parameters (atmospheric chemical potential, outgoing long-wave radiation, and surface skin temperature) and the Ultra-Low-Frequency (ULF) geomagnetic field data. The results strongly indicated that the electric field channel and electromagnetic emission could be regarded as the main factors that triggered PEIAs during the earthquake preparation phase.

presentations.presentation_title: A Machine-Learning-Aided Framework for Regional GNSS Water Vapor Tomography
presentations.abstract: Water vapor is a key component of the atmosphere and plays an essential role in weather systems and regional climate processes. However, its three-dimensional (3D) distribution is difficult to observe with sufficient resolution. Ground-based Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) observations provide continuous and all-weather measurements of zenith total delay (ZTD), making them a valuable data source for atmospheric water vapor tomography. In this study, we investigate a GNSS-based water vapor tomography approach using machine learning techniques. Slant water vapor observations are derived from station-wise ZTD time series, and the atmosphere is discretized into multi-layered voxels. A machine learning model is introduced to infer voxel-based three-dimensional water vapor distributions from GNSS-derived slant water vapor observations under ray geometry constraints. This approach helps reduce the reliance on strong prior constraints commonly adopted in conventional linear inversion methods. By implicitly learning the inversion regularization from data, the proposed framework provides a data-driven approach to stabilize the inversion without relying on strongly prescribed prior constraints. Numerical simulation experiments are conducted to evaluate the feasibility of the proposed framework. The results indicate that the proposed method can produce stable and physically reasonable three-dimensional water vapor structures. These findings suggest that integrating GNSS-derived observations into a machine-learning-based inversion scheme provides a promising framework for regional water vapor tomography.

presentations.presentation_title: Pre-earthquake Ionospheric Signals Observed by Total Electron Content and Electron Density Profiles Before the 28 March 2025 M7.7 Myanmar Earthquake
presentations.abstract: This study utilizes the total electron content (TEC) from the global ionosphere map (GIM) and GNSS radio occultation (RO) electron density profiles from FORMOSAT-7/COSMIC-2 (F7/C2) to investigate pre-earthquake ionospheric signals (PEISs) associated with the M7.7 Myanmar earthquake on 28 March 2025. Temporal and spatial analyses reveal that a significant and persistent TEC reduction occurred specifically over the epicenter on 25 March, 3 days before the Myanmar earthquake, which suggests that PEISs have been observed. F7/C2 observations further illustrate that the ionospheric F2 peak electron density (NmF2) decreased by approximately 30–80% and the peak height (hmF2) descended by about 50 km during the PEIS period. The distance between northern and southern crests of equatorial ionization anomaly along the earthquake longitude shows that westward seismo-generated electric fields resulted in the significant TEC decrease, NmF2 reduction, and hmF2 descent.

presentations.presentation_title: Creation of Sustainable Disaster Mitigation Science
presentations.abstract: In the event of meteorological disasters such as heavy rains and typhoons, information on rainfall, wind speed, etc. is made public in advance, albeit with uncertainties, encouraging society to respond. Society, in turn, develops preventative measures while taking into account the uncertainty of predictions. Meanwhile, information on earthquakes and tsunamis is currently available only after they have occurred, with very little advance information available. Even in the case of large earthquakes of magnitude 7 or greater, forecasts available during normal times, one week, three days, one day, several hours, one hour, immediately before the seismic wave arrival, and 20 minutes before the tsunami arrival would be expected to facilitate advance preparations and damage mitigation actions for individuals and businesses. Furthermore, as seen in the Boso Typhoon and Noto Earthquake, information on disaster damage during and immediately after a disaster is scarce. This information shortage is particularly severe at night, during severe weather, when power outages occur, and when other factors, such as the spread of infectious diseases and nuclear accidents, combine to make appropriate disaster response activities difficult. The use of accurate forecasting and disaster monitoring information in addition to conventional weather information and earthquake early warnings is expected to further reduce economic and human losses. Therefore, we have conceived a world-first initiative to develop a system that extracts information useful for disaster prediction, monitoring, and reconstruction support from Earth observation big data, as well as a crisis response navigator using this system, and to implement it in society. We aim to create a sustainable science for disaster mitigation that contributes to the realization of a disaster-resilient society.

presentations.presentation_title: Physical-informed ETAS Model and Its Application to Reservoir Earthquakes
presentations.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Epidemic-Type Aftershock Sequence (ETAS) model is one of the most widely used statistical models applied to earthquake prediction. As a statistical method, ETAS and its extension are all based on earthquake catalogs that usually ignore the physical mechanism. The ETAS model may not describe seismicity well when the regional stress changes frequently, e.g., reservoirs, shale gas extraction, and wastewater injection. To address this, we propose a new earthquake probabilistic forecast model by integrating regional stress evolution, i.e., Stress-informed ETAS model. We applied this new model to reservoir earthquakes in the Jinsha River, China. The detailed results will be shown in our presentation.

presentations.presentation_title: Possible Lithosphere-Atmosphere-Ionosphere Coupling in the Occasion of the Present Campi Flegrei Caldera (italy) Unrest
presentations.institution: Italian National Institute of Geophysics and Vulcanology
presentations.abstract: Campi Flegrei Caldera is an active volcano in Italy, located in a densely populated area near the city of Naples, with a history of volcanic activity, as evidenced by Ancient Roman artefacts. The Caldera was formed by an explosive eruption that occurred about 36’000 years ago, and other eruptions occurred in the twelfth century. Part of the caldera is submerged beneath the Gulf of Pozzuoli, increasing the potential risk of an eruption due to the violent interaction of magma and water. From 2005, the GNSS station RITE (close to Pozzuoli) recorded a continuous uplift of the Caldera that exceeded 1.3 meters in 2025, and from 2019 the area is characterised by an increase of seismicity, with larger events occurring on 20-05-2024 (Md = 4.4), 13-03-2025 (Md = 4.6 and Md=4.4) and 30-06-2025 (Md = 4.6).In this work, we analysed climatological atmospheric data, extracting anomalies from several physical and chemical parameters related to atmospheric status and composition. In addition, we explored satellite magnetic data from the ESA Swarm mission to search for potential ionospheric disturbances to critically discussed eventual link with the activity in the Campi Flegrei Caldera.We identified an increase in sulphur dioxide anomalies in correspondence with the increase in seismic activity, likely due to degassing from the complex hydrothermal system. We also discussed an anomalous magnetic signal recorded in the ionosphere in light of a possible source from the volcanic activity. We consider, in fact, that the earthquake magnitudes of the events that occurred in 2024 and 2025 are too low to influence the ionosphere, but their nature is volcanic rather than tectonic, possibly due to magma rising under the caldera. Consequently, the source of the possible lithosphere, atmosphere, and ionosphere coupling would be driven by volcanic activity.

presentations.presentation_title: Relation between Ionosphere and Ground motion
presentations.institution: International Research Center for Space and Planetary environment Science
presentations.abstract: We discuss the frequency spectrum of slant gauge data for several earthquakes(M>7) which occurred in Japan.Our final goal is to predict the location of the epicenter and the day of the occurrence. Toward our final goal. We are studying daily variation of Maximum electron density (NmF2) y observed by four ionosondes in Japan operated by (NICT) and ground motion observed with the slant gauges distributed over Japan, managed by (NIED). 1 sec data was downloaded from NIED. frequency spectrum, and Power Spectrum Density (PSD) were calculated from Raw data. So far, we studied 5 earthquakes of M greater than 7. Under the idea that ionosphere is modified by the DC electric field (Dynamo field) generated between 100-200 km where the neutral density plays a fundamental role. We assume that the electric field is enhanced by the plasma irregularities which is caused by the breaking of neutral waves. The neutral waves are triggered by the ground motion. Accordingly, we started the relationship between the ground motion and ionosphere variation. We found that both NmF2 and PSD shows special feature five days before the large earthquake occurs. In this presentation we discuss the physical mechanism of NmF2 and PSD behavior, by referring a paper by Sholz et al. ReferencesSholz, C.H., L.R. Sykes, and Y. P. presentations.presentation_title: A Revised Automatic Detection Scheme to Identify Equatorial Plasma Bubbles Observed by Advanced Ionospheric Probe Onboard Formosat-5 Satellite
presentations.abstract: An automatic scheme to detect equatorial plasma bubbles had been developed for Ionospheric Plasma and Electrodynamics Instrument (IPEI) onboard ROCSAT-1 satellite which was in a 35° inclination orbit at 600 km altitude (Su et al., 2006). However, some mis-identifications could be found in the southern hemisphere of the negative magnetic declination longitudinal region during June solstice when the scheme was applied for data measured by Advanced Ionospheric Probe (AIP) onboard the FORMOSAT-5 satellite which was in a 98.28° inclination sun-synchronous circular orbit at 720 km altitude. The mis-identifications seems to relate to mid-latitude ring ionospheric troughs (Karpachev, 2019). In this presentation, global seasonal patterns of the equatorial plasma bubbles from FORMOSAT-5/AIP data during 2018 to 2025 were re-generated by a revised scheme like the rate of change of density index (RODI) by Jin et al. (2019) and are similar to the patterns obtained by ROCSAT1/IPEI data during 1999-2003.
presentations.session_title: Natural Hazards and Their Multi-sphere Coupling: from the Lithosphere to Space

presentations.presentation_title: The Lithosphere-atmosphere-ionosphere Coupling During Landslides
presentations.abstract: Numerous studies have demonstrated that acoustic waves can be generated during the preparatory stage of landslides. However, whether these acoustic signals can propagate upward through the atmosphere and trigger ionospheric disturbances remains insufficiently understood. This study aims to investigate the role of landslide-induced acoustic waves in driving lithosphere–atmosphere–ionosphere (LAI) coupling processes. We analyzed geomagnetic observations collected in the vicinity of landslide-prone regions and identified out-of-phase variations in the geomagnetic field components. Such signatures indicate the existence of atmospheric electric currents, suggesting active electrodynamic coupling in the atmosphere. Similar geomagnetic and ionospheric responses were also observed following the acoustic waves generated by the 2024 Hualien earthquake, providing an independent validation of the proposed mechanism. In addition, acoustic wave activity was found to induce perturbations in total electron content (TEC). Because landslides typically originate from spatially localized source regions, the resulting acoustic waves propagate radially outward. By tracking TEC disturbances, we observed that these perturbations migrate away from the landslide source region, a pattern that is consistently confirmed by satellite observations. These results collectively suggest that acoustic waves play a key role in initiating LAI coupling prior to landslide occurrence. Our findings indicate that landslide-associated acoustic waves constitute a dominant causal mechanism governing cross-sphere coupling during landslide processes. Importantly, the detection of pre-landslide acoustic signals and their associated ionospheric responses highlights a promising pathway for developing acoustic-based approaches for landslide tracing, localization, and early warning.
presentations.session_title: Natural Hazards and Their Multi-sphere Coupling: from the Lithosphere to Space

presentations.presentation_title: Disturbances of Ionospheric Total Electron Content During January 2025 California Wildfires
presentations.abstract: In this study, we analyzed the ionospheric total electron content (TEC) data derived from ground-based Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receivers at the continental United States during the Southern California wildfires in January 2025. The ionospheric disturbances were most prominent on 8 January, exhibiting amplitudes of approximately 1 total electron content unit (TECU) and a period of ~25 minutes. Comparisons between the ionospheric TEC disturbances and the atmospheric brightness temperature observations from the Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) onboard the GOES-16 (Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite 16) and the Atmospheric Infrared Sounder (AIRS) aboard the Aqua satellite suggest that atmospheric gravity waves, occurred over the vicinity of the wildfires, played an important role in driving the ionospheric disturbances over California during this severe wildfire event.
presentations.session_title: Natural Hazards and Their Multi-sphere Coupling: from the Lithosphere to Space

presentations.presentation_title: From the Lithosphere to Space: Earthquake- and Tsunami-related Electromagnetic Disturbances Toward Space Seismology
presentations.abstract: Earthquakes and tsunamis generate disturbances that propagate far beyond the solid Earth, coupling the lithosphere, atmosphere, ionosphere, and geospace through a variety of mechanical and electromagnetic processes. Over the past decade, my research has focused on identifying and interpreting such earthquake- and tsunami-related electromagnetic disturbances using coordinated ground-based and spaceborne observations, with the aim of establishing a unified framework that I refer to as space seismology. One key outcome of this work is the identification and characterization of the tsunami ionospheric hole, a localized and persistent depletion of ionospheric electron density formed above propagating tsunamis. Observations using GNSS total electron content, satellite plasma measurements, and complementary ground-based data demonstrate that this structure is not a simple wave-like perturbation, but a dynamically maintained feature resulting from tsunami-driven acoustic–gravity waves and associated electrodynamic responses. The ionospheric hole provides a clear and physically interpretable signature of tsunami propagation over the open ocean, detectable at distances far from the seismic source. In parallel, my studies have examined earthquake-related electromagnetic and geomagnetic variations observed on the ground and in near-Earth space, including ionospheric plasma perturbations and current systems excited by seismic and tsunami-generated atmospheric waves. These results highlight that the ionosphere and geospace respond as an integrated dynamical system to lithospheric forcing, rather than as passive receivers of isolated signals. Building on these findings, space seismology is proposed as an extension of conventional seismology that exploits the ionosphere and geospace as remote, wide-area sensors of seismic and tsunami activity. With the increasing availability of dense GNSS networks, real-time ionospheric monitoring, and future satellite constellations, this approach offers a promising pathway toward early tsunami detection and improved situational awareness for hazard mitigation.

presentations.presentation_title: A Linear Inverse Modeling Approach to Pacific-Indian Ocean Causality Based on Liang-Kleeman Information Flow
presentations.abstract: Causal interactions between major climate modes are central to understanding the evolution of climate variability. We present a linear inverse modeling (LIM) framework that explicitly accounts for both memoryless and persistent stochastic forcing in a cyclostationary system to estimate causality based on Liang–Kleeman (LK) information flow. Embedding LK diagnostics within a generalized LIM allows a quantitative separation of the contributions from internal dynamics and stochastic processes to the growth and damping of variability.The method is applied to re-examine causal interactions between El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) using monthly sea surface temperature anomaly data and the Dipole Mode Index. Results show that inter-basin information transfer from the IOD to the Pacific is generally weaker than Pacific self-causality overall but exhibits strong spatial and seasonal structure. The IOD excites variability in the eastern Pacific while stabilizing the central Pacific during boreal autumn, partially offsetting intrinsic Pacific dynamics, consistent with contrasting mechanisms of canonical ENSO and ENSO Modoki events.Stochastic forcing dominates the buildup of Pacific SST variability. Persistent noise, potentially related to Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), provides robust excitation with characteristic timescales of 1–2 months over the major Niño areas, suggesting the potential pathway linking the MJO to ENSO. High-frequency forcing shows stronger spatiotemporal variability. In coastal Niño regions, atmospheric white-noise forcing may act as a precursor to basin-scale events. These results highlight the importance of stochastic processes in causal influence, a mechanism not explicitly emphasized in earlier studies.
presentations.session_title: Advances in Causality Analysis for Earth System Science: Methods and Applications

presentations.presentation_title: Subseasonal-to-seasonal Causal Influence of Antecedent Soil Moisture on the Summer Precipitation Over the Contiguous United States
presentations.institution: Nanjing University of Information Science and Techonology
presentations.abstract: Assessment of the causal relation between atmosphere and land is a continuing challenge in hydrometeorology. In this study, we introduce a recently developed method of causality analysis into hydrometeorological research, namely, the Liang information flow analysis. Different from the existing statistical formalisms, it is grounded in physics, and has been rigorously established from first principles. The method is first validated with the benchmark hydrological bucket model as examined by Ombadi et al. (2020, Water Resources Research, 56, e2020WR027251) which left unsatisfactory four other major causal inference methods, showing that it is able to accurately recover the embedded causal structure. It is then applied to investigate the causality from antecedent soil moisture to summer precipitation within the subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) timescales across the contiguous United States. Two hotspots of S2S soil moisture–precipitation causality are identified in the Southwest and Northwest. Notably, these regions exhibit contrasting causality evolutions with respect to lead time (led by soil moisture), providing different degrees of precipitation predictability across S2S timescales. Sensitivity experiments in S2S precipitation prediction confirm that soil moisture at lead times exhibiting stronger causality contributes more to skill improvement, underscoring the importance of accurately identifying causal lead times to leverage land surface memory in extended-range forecasts. Further analysis reveals different causal pathways in terms of evapotranspiration between the two hotspots. In the Southwest, evapotranspiration acts as a mediator between soil moisture and precipitation, whereas in the Northwest, this mediating role is absent due to a lack of soil moisture constraint on evapotranspiration.
presentations.session_title: Advances in Causality Analysis for Earth System Science: Methods and Applications

presentations.presentation_title: Causality as a Real Physical Notion Ab Initio, and Its Applications in Geosciences
presentations.abstract: Causality analysis is an important task of scientific research across disciplines. Though traditionally formulated as a statistical problem, in terms of information flow/transfer it has been found to be a real notion in physics that can be derived ab initio. A comprehensive study with generic systems has been fulfilled, with explicit formulas attained in closed form (Liang, 2016). These formulas are invariant upon nonlinear coordinate transformation, indicating that the so-obtained information flow should be an intrinsic physical property. In the linear limit, its maximum likelihood estimator is concise in form, involving only the commonly used statistics, i.e., sample covariances. A corollary is that causation implies correlation, but the converse does not hold, expressing the long standing philosophical debate ever since Berkeley (1710) in a transparent mathematical expression. The above rigorous formalism has been validated with benchmark systems like baker transformation and Hénon map, and with causal networks in extreme situations such as those with nodes almost synchronized. They have also been applied to real world problems in the diverse disciplines such as climate science, dynamic meteorology, turbulence, neuroscience, financial economics, quantum mechanics, etc., with interesting new findings. For example, Stips et al. (2016) found that, while CO 2 emission does drive the recent global warming, on a paleoclimate scale, it is global warming that drives the CO 2 emission; PNA, a teleconnection pattern related to the inclement weather in North America, may trace part of its origin to a rather limited local marginal sea far away in Asia. If time permits, I will also present an ongoing application to the development of causal AI algorithms to overcome the interpretability crisis, and a recent exercise with such an algorithm in the forecasting of El Niño Modoki, a climate mode linked to hazards in far-flung regions of the globe.
presentations.session_title: Advances in Causality Analysis for Earth System Science: Methods and Applications

presentations.presentation_title: Background Aridity Dependent Modification of Land-Atmosphere Feedbacks During Compound Drought-Heatwave Events
presentations.abstract: Compound drought-heatwave events (CDHEs) are among the most damaging climate extremes, arising from the concurrence of two impactful extremes and resulting in devastating impacts on socioeconomic systems. Their increasing frequency and intensity under climate change highlight the need to better understand the physical processes governing their development. In particular, land-atmosphere feedbacks, including soil moisture-temperature interactions, are widely recognized as playing a central role in the local dynamics leading to the onset of CDHEs. Yet, how these feedbacks behave during compound extremes, and how their characteristics differ from those under normal conditions, remains insufficiently understood due to the inability of most current methods to disentangle causal feedbacks from correlations, especially under non-stationary and extreme conditions.We use the Liang-Kleeman information flow, a causality formalism based on the entropy budget in dynamical systems, to quantify directional land-atmosphere interactions between normal conditions and CDHEs at the global scale using ERA5 reanalysis data (1950-2024). We find that soil moisture-temperature coupling changes during CDHEs; however, the coupling response differs depending on background water availability. Specifically, the coupling strengthens in humid regions during CDHEs, whereas the opposite response occurs in arid regions.

presentations.presentation_title: Exploring Factors That Affect Japanese Older Adults’ Risk Perception and Preparedness for Earthquakes
presentations.abstract: We examine how cognitive, emotional, and psychosocial factors interact to influence earthquake risk perception and preparedness among Japanese older adults residing in Pacific Ocean-adjacent prefectures with high seismic risk (Fukurai et al. 2026). Perceptions of earthquakes and lived experiences elicit emotional and cognitive responses that shape disaster preparedness behaviors. Older adults, having lived through multiple hazard events, are often assumed to have higher risk perception (awareness) and therefore greater preparedness. However, this assumption overlooks age-related changes in emotional processing and cognition. While hazard experience increases knowledge, preparedness is not driven by knowledge alone. Many older adults recognize that disasters are possible yet underestimate their personal vulnerability, a phenomenon known as optimism bias.Globally, older adults experience disproportionately higher mortality, morbidity, and long-term displacement during natural disasters. Physical limitations, chronic illness, mobility impairments, sensory loss, and reliance on medication or caregiving infrastructure further increase vulnerability during emergencies. At the same time, socio-emotional aging research suggests that older adults may prioritize emotional regulation and maintain more positive outlooks, potentially dampening perceived personal risk despite objective vulnerability.By focusing on barriers beyond knowledge, such as optimism bias, emotional regulation, and lived experience, this work seeks to disentangle the complex mechanisms underlying preparedness behavior in later life. Understanding these dynamics is critical for designing age-appropriate risk communication strategies and preparedness interventions that account for both psychosocial and structural vulnerabilities in aging populations.Fukurai, M., A. Yong, L. G. Ludwig, B. Bocekli, P. Wang, S. Matsushima, K. Hudson, and S. Stanley (2026). Real-Time Public Reactions to Earthquakes via an Earthquake Early Warning Platform in Japan: Implications for Risk Perception, Seism. Res. Lett., 97, 2b.
presentations.session_title: Interdisciplinary Strategies to Advancing Pre-disaster Measures and Resilience Against Large Earthquakes

presentations.presentation_title: Behavioral Science as a Key to Advancing Pre-disaster Measures Against Earthquake Hazards
presentations.abstract: Despite major advances in earthquake research and widespread disaster education in schools and public seminars, pre-disaster measures at the household and community levels remain limited in Japan. This gap indicates that the main bottleneck in disaster risk reduction (DRR) is not a lack of scientific knowledge or awareness, but the difficulty of translating awareness into concrete action. In this presentation, I argue that accelerating pre-disaster measures requires placing behavioral science at the center of disaster preparedness and mitigation strategies, and that health communication provides an effective framework.In public health, risk information alone is not expected to change behavior. Instead, interventions are designed by treating human action itself as the primary target and by embedding preventive measures into daily life, social systems, and existing support structures. Such interventions are often coordinated at the national level, and their effectiveness is evaluated using systematic indicators. In contrast, in DRR against earthquake hazards, several critical issues remain: the behavioral outcomes of interventions are rarely monitored; systematic interventions across societal levels are insufficient; and most disaster communication studies have focused on awareness or intention rather than actual behavioral change.Our ongoing initiatives design and test interventions in collaboration with health professionals, using health-communication-based approaches such as integrating earthquake safety messages into maternal and child health programs. By collecting scientific evidence of effectiveness, these methods can be refined and applied more broadly. Such efforts aim to systematize “DRR communication” and to establish structured intervention and support systems for DRR at the individual and community levels.From this perspective, earthquake hazard research and advanced observation systems, including real-time monitoring and emerging techniques such as AI-based anomaly detection, play a critical but supporting role. Their societal value is realized only when embedded in social systems and linked with behavioral science, translating scientific knowledge into concrete actions.
presentations.session_title: Interdisciplinary Strategies to Advancing Pre-disaster Measures and Resilience Against Large Earthquakes

presentations.presentation_title: Pre-earthquake b Value Variation Indicates the Rupture of the 2008 Wenchuan Earthquake
presentations.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: Earthquakes are among the most destructive natural hazards, yet forecasting their occurrence and impacts remains a major scientific challenge. The 2008 Mw 8.0 Wenchuan earthquake, the most damaging intra-plate event of this century, ruptured the northern Longmenshan fault zone (LMSFZ) at the eastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau. Here, we report the spatiotemporal evolution of b values along the LMSFZ before the mainshock. The b value characterizes the relative proportion of small to large earthquakes and is inversely related to differential stress on a fault, making it a potential proxy for subsurface stress state and seismic hazard. In this work, from the b-values, the rupture segment exhibits lower stress and lower hazard relative to adjacent unruptured segments, yet the temporal variation of b-values reveals progressive stress accumulation and rising hazard prior to failure. This contrast may reflect underlying structural heterogeneity along the fault. Crucially, regions of pronounced b-value decrease coincide with areas of large coseismic slip and high seismic intensity and correlate positively with coseismic velocity changes. We propose that b-value evolution records differential stress loading along the segmented fault, delineating asperities and zones of serious damage. These findings enhance our understanding of earthquake preparation and rupture mechanics, and aid in identifying high-hazard areas for seismic risk reduction.

presentations.presentation_title: Personalized Evacuation Support System: Augmenting Situational Awareness via Relevance-Driven Sensor Networks
presentations.institution: Graduate School of Interdisciplinary Information Studies, The University of Tokyo
presentations.abstract: Human protective behavior during disasters is often constrained by the limits of natural perception: individuals may fail to detect early hazard cues or rapidly evolving environmental conditions. Developed at the University of Tokyo’s Earthquake Research Institute, this system extends human sensory awareness by integrating a relevance-driven sensor network designed to identify hazards earlier than users can perceive themselves. Rather than relying solely on hyperlocal data, the system selects the most situationally relevant sensor inputs (including remote sensors associated with family members, dependents, or critical assets) thereby providing extended senses that reflect not only the user’s physical surroundings but also their social and emotional responsibilities.Conventional hazard notification systems commonly issue alerts that are geographically broad or ambiguous, unintentionally involving individuals who are not affected. This phenomenon reduces perceived relevance, undermines trust, and contributes to alert fatigue. By contrast, the proposed system grounds hazard information in a personalized set of sensors chosen for their relevance to the user’s risk context, thus enhancing the credibility and personal ownership of the information.The proposed framework relies on two core mechanisms to eliminate cognitive waste and secure time to act. First, self-data acquisition leverages a network of proximate and remote sensors to generate high-fidelity, trustable environmental insights without requiring users to verify external information sources. Second, on-demand information selection employs agent-based conversational interfaces to filter noise and deliver concise, context-specific safety actions. The research further investigates the trustful acquisition of personal attributes such as mobility constraints to optimize this guidance.By uniting relevance-weighted sensory extension with cognitively lightweight guidance, the system accelerates the transition from hazard detection to protective action. The ultimate objective is to stabilize situational understanding early enough to not only enhance individual safety but also empower users to shift their focus toward prosocial behavior, thereby strengthening resilience at both household and community levels.

presentations.presentation_title: Integrated Gnss, Insar, and Multi-layer Compaction Observations for Quantifying Coastal Land Subsidence in Western Taiwan
presentations.institution: Green Environmental Engineering Consultant Co. Ltd
presentations.abstract: Land subsidence in coastal alluvial plains is characterized by strong spatial heterogeneity, depth-dependent deformation, and close coupling with groundwater dynamics. The Changhua–Yunlin coastal plain in western Taiwan has experienced persistent subsidence driven by long-term groundwater extraction, making it an ideal area to evaluate integrated geodetic monitoring approaches. This study applies a multi-sensor geodetic framework integrating continuous GNSS observations, precise leveling surveys, multi-temporal Sentinel-1 InSAR, and multi-layer compaction monitoring wells to quantify land subsidence across surface and subsurface scales. Displacement time series from 26 continuous GNSS stations provide three-dimensional deformation, while over 1,000 km of leveling surveys offer high-accuracy vertical control. Regional deformation patterns are mapped using Small Baseline Subset (SBAS) InSAR processing. In addition, magnetic-ring multi-layer compaction wells directly measure depth-resolved compaction within aquifer and aquitard systems. Cross-comparison of GNSS, leveling, and InSAR results shows strong consistency in vertical deformation rates, confirming the reliability of satellite-based observations for regional subsidence monitoring. Results indicate that subsidence in Changhua is generally localized and moderate, with typical rates of 1–3 cm yr⁻¹, whereas Yunlin exhibits broader and more severe subsidence, reaching 3–5 cm yr⁻¹ in some areas. Long-term observations reveal cumulative subsidence exceeding 2 m since the early 1990s. Compaction data further demonstrate that subsidence is often dominated by specific aquifer systems, with significant contributions from deeper layers and delayed consolidation effects. The integrated geodetic framework enhances interpretation of surface deformation, constrains subsidence mechanisms at depth, and provides a transferable methodology for monitoring land subsidence in vulnerable coastal and deltaic regions worldwide.
presentations.session_title: Coastal Subsidence and Relative Sea-level Rise

presentations.presentation_title: Land Subsidence and Relative Sea-Level Rise in Bangkok: Implications for Flood Hazard
presentations.institution: Department of Survey Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, Chulalongkorn University,
presentations.abstract: Bangkok and the Greater Bangkok area are highly vulnerable to flooding due to their low elevation and ongoing land subsidence. In addition to groundwater-induced subsidence, regional land motion has been influenced by post-seismic deformation following the 2004 Sumatra–Andaman earthquake. Continuous GNSS observations reveal persistent vertical subsidence across Thailand, including Bangkok. This study integrates GNSS and InSAR observations from 2018 to 2024 to estimate absolute surface velocities relative to mean sea level. By aligning InSAR-derived relative velocities with the GNSS reference frame, we obtain reliable subsidence rates that capture both deep-seated tectonic processes and shallow effects. Results indicate that post-seismic subsidence in the Bangkok area is ongoing but diminishing. The combined effects of land subsidence and sea-level rise significantly increase flood risk, highlighting the need for accurate subsidence monitoring for coastal hazard assessment.
presentations.session_title: Coastal Subsidence and Relative Sea-level Rise

presentations.presentation_title: Incorporating Short Term Transients Into VLM and RSLR Projections: an Example from Aotearoa/new Zealand
presentations.abstract: Improved estimates of national scale Vertical Land Movement (VLM) and their influence on Relative Sea Level Rise (RSLR) projections are critical to support local and national coastal hazard management. In order to extract high spatial resolution estimate of VLM, geodetic datasets (InSAR and GNSS) collected over the last 20-30 years are commonly used to estimate current rates of VLM and project them into the future. However, shorter term transients from anthropogenic processes, tectonics (earthquake cycle deformation) and/or volcanism, may locally perturb longer term rates for years to decades raising questions around the validity of using shorter term geodetic estimates. However, capturing the uncertainty around shorter term transients in RSLR projections is challenging. In New Zealand, projections have been produced by coupling SSP scenarios with interseismic VLM estimates derived from Envisat at 2-km intervals around the coast. However, in the last 20-years, the New Zealand coastline has been effected by multiple moderate to large earthquakes, as well as significant post-seismic transients following the 2016 Mw 7.8 Kaikoura earthquake, which are not accounted for in current projections. Furthermore, the rapid growth of urban centres along the coast has led to significant local variations in VLM associated with urban loading on reclaimed and/or subsidence prone land. Here we present a full suite of new RSLR projections for the 15,000 km coastline of New Zealand which combines existing interseismic VLM estimates derived from Envisat with a newly derived VLM dataset derived from Sentinel-1. The new projections include the effects of co-seismic VLM from earthquakes that have occurred since 2005 and provide an approach to account for post-seismic transients and urban loading which may only influence VLM rates over the next few years to decades.
presentations.session_title: Coastal Subsidence and Relative Sea-level Rise

presentations.presentation_title: Land Subsidence and Geosphere Environments in Subsiding Coastal Plain, Japan
presentations.abstract: The Japanese archipelago experiences persistent ground deformation associated with active tectonics. In addition to these natural processes, anthropogenic land subsidence has become a critical issue in many lowland areas. In the Alluvial plains of Japan, thick clay deposits are distributed, making these plains particularly susceptible to subsidence caused by intensive groundwater extraction. Understanding the interactions between ground deformation and the geosphere environment is essential for sustainable environmental management and disaster mitigation in lowland and coastal areas. This study presents two representative case studies from major subsiding coastal plains in Japan: the Kujukuri Plain in Chiba and the Echigo Plain in Niigata. In the Kujukuri Plain, three-dimensional numerical modeling was applied to evaluate the effects of land subsidence and subsequent flood-control infrastructure on salinization of shallow groundwater along tidal rivers. The results - suggested that these factors may enhance inland saltwater intrusion. In the Echigo Plain, localized subsidence areas identified through ground deformation analyses were compared with the spatiotemporal distributions of subsurface geology. By analyzing detailed subsurface stratigraphy, significant subsidence was identified, mainly in areas underlain by thick clay and silt layers, highlighting the importance of understanding consolidation processes. However, some subsiding zones could not be fully explained by geological conditions alone, suggesting that surface activities, including land use and groundwater management, exert a substantial influence on subsidence.
presentations.session_title: Coastal Subsidence and Relative Sea-level Rise

presentations.presentation_title: Earthquake Occurrence Along the Arabian Gulf - Relationships with Seasonal Changes in Atmospheric and Hydrological Crustal Loading
presentations.abstract: The collision of the northward-moving Arabian tectonic plate with the Eurasian tectonic plate causes lithospheric compressional stress in the Arabian Gulf region, which results in recurrent earthquake activity. Here, to evaluate whether any earthquake seasonality can be observed in the Arabian Gulf region, we use reliable catalogues maintained by the USGS (United States Geological Survey) and ISC (International Seismological Center). To avoid any potential issues resulting from incompleteness of data, we focused on earthquakes with a magnitude greater than M5. Aftershocks were omitted using the Gardner and Knopoff method, which considers both space and time to remove the dependent earthquakes. Owing to the limited number of large events in the datasets, the annual seismicity pattern was studied using three-month bins.It is found that earthquake occur more often in the summer months of July, August and September. Two statistical tests (Shuster & Ohtake, and Nakahara) were performed to assess the significance of the observed seismicity pattern. In both tests, the seasonality is statistically significant at the ~93% confidence level. The greater number of earthquakes during the summer season can be attributed to reduced atmospheric and hydrological crustal loading, which enhances Coulomb Failure Stress (CFS). Seasonal atmospheric pressure varies significantly in this region with an observed average pressure difference of 25 hPa between the summer (lower pressure) and winter (higher pressure), while hydrological loading from seasonal rainfall is in phase with the atmospheric pattern. Combined atmospheric and hydrological loading is therefore proposed to increase earthquake potential occurrence during the summer months, and likewise reduces earthquake potential in winter, around the Arabian Gulf.
presentations.session_title: Natural Hazards and Disaster Risk

presentations.presentation_title: Probabilistic Forecasting of Volcanic Multiphase Multihazards
presentations.abstract: Probabilistic Volcanic Hazard Analysis (PVHA) is in its relative infancy, largely due to the multi-phase and multi-hazard nature of volcanic eruptions. The problem to be solved is in forecasting which hazard(s) may impact a specific point (usually that of some piece of critical infrastructure, such as a bridge, building, or pylon) with what intensity, in what combination(s) and with what likelihood. Here we present a methodology to dynamically forecast probabilistic impacts from multiple hazards at specified locations. The workflow uses a semi-Markov process to forecast intra-eruption durations and quiescence’s, along with the style of future eruptive phases. Conditional on the phase style, we probabilistically forecast the occurrence (or not) of various hazardous phenomena and their intensities / magnitudes. These are converted into spatial-probability footprints using semi-empirical models and combined using the forecast phase path(s) to give the probability of a hazard exceeding a given intensity impacting a location within a specified time window.

presentations.presentation_title: Control of Crater and Edifice Morphology on the Emplacement of the 1814 Pyroclastic Flow Deposits of Mayon Volcano
presentations.institution: National Institute of Geological Sciences, University of the Philippines Diliman
presentations.abstract: Pyroclastic flows (PFs) are among the most destructive and deadliest volcanic hazards, yet they were often poorly understood in historical eruptions prior to the advent of instrumental monitoring. The 1 February 1814 eruption of Mayon Volcano was a volcanic explosivity index (VEI) 4 event. It generated extensive PFs down the volcano’s southern flanks and devastated communities along their path. In this study, we reconstructed the PFs of Mayon’s 1814 eruption using Titan2D with constraints from field data and historical accounts. A series of numerical simulations explores how the flow extent and deposit thickness of a simulated PF are influenced by the changes in basal friction angle and source direction, representing inclined versus vertical column-collapse scenarios controlled by crater morphology. An important input to these simulations is the DEM, representing Mayon’s edifice morphology. From trials, a basal friction angle of 12° produces the simulation that best matches the mapped distribution and runout distances (~7-9 km) of the 1814 ignimbrite deposits. Simulations incorporating an inclined gas thrust region of an eruption plume generate directional emplacement of PFs, while a control simulation assuming a vertical fountain collapse produces radially distributed flows inconsistent with field observations. The results of our study show that the inclination of the gas thrust region of an eruption plume, which is controlled by crater morphology, significantly influenced the directional characteristics of the 1814 PFs, and can be a critical factor in present-day hazard assessment. This study demonstrates how Titan2D can be effective for reconstructing historical eruptions at stratovolcanoes with limited data and highlights the important role of crater geometry in generating pyroclastic flow hazard maps.

presentations.presentation_title: Compounding Coastal Extremes from Tropical Cyclone and Marine Heatwave: Subdistrict-level Multi-hazard Risk Profile for Coastal India
presentations.abstract: Coastal India is increasingly susceptible to compounding maritime and atmospheric extremes, yet traditional risk frameworks often overlook granular socio-economic disparities and the synergistic nature of multi-hazard events. Our study presents a comprehensive subdistrict-level assessment of coastal risk by integrating Tropical Cyclone (TC) and Marine Heatwave (MHW) impacts. The TC hazard assessment utilizes a novel quasi-Lagrangian approach to investigate co-occurring wind and rainfall extremes (1979–2020), while MHW hazards are quantified for ocean areas immediately adjacent to the coast. For vulnerability, we evaluate 50 indicators across six dimensions—social, economic, household amenities/assets, household infrastructure, physical (geomorphic), and public infrastructure—leveraging Census of India, OpenStreetMap, and high-resolution terrain data. A significant methodological advancement is the application of Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NNMF) and the PAreto Ranking-based Method for Aggregate Relative Scoring (PARMAR) algorithm. Unlike Principal Component Analysis, which can produce negative loadings that are difficult to interpret in a socio-economic context, the NNMF ensures strictly additive, non-negative components. A new objective, non-parametric PARMAR algorithm further eliminates subjective weighting while preserving ordinal ranking logic. Key findings show peak TC hazards concentrated along the eastern seaboard (Odisha, West Bengal, and northern Andhra Pradesh), while MHW frequency peaks along the South-West (Kerala) and North-East coasts at nearly three events annually. Vulnerability hotspots in the Sundarbans and coastal Odisha significantly amplify these extremes due to fragile housing and limited emergency accessibility. The results highlight a critical interplay: MHWs fuel rapid TC intensification, whereas TCs can temporarily alleviate ocean heat through vertical mixing. By addressing subdistrict-level heterogeneities, this study provides a robust evidence base for moving beyond generic state-level planning to targeting specific intersections of environmental exposure and socio-economic fragility in disaster risk reduction strategies. Importantly, this methodology is generic, globally transferable, and the NNMF-PARMAR framework is well-suited for diverse Multi-Attribute Decision Making problems beyond vulnerability assessment.

presentations.presentation_title: Using Tree Rings for Early Detection of Catastrophic Landslides: Case Studies from Poland and Italy
presentations.abstract: We examined six slopes, three in Poland (the Western Carpathians and the Sudetes) and three in Italy (the Northern and Southern Apennines), which had either experienced past catastrophic landslides or were considered prone to catastrophic reactivation. For each site, past landslide activity was reconstructed. The analysis focused on tree-ring eccentricity in trees growing on the investigated slopes, using the percentage eccentricity index method. This approach allowed us to identify annual variations in eccentricity for individual trees and to date landslide events based on the collective response of tree populations at each site. The resulting data provided proxy evidence of temporal changes in landslide activity, indicating that all studied slopes had been affected by frequent landsliding in the past, with recurrence intervals ranging from 2.0 to 7.1 years. Furthermore, in four slopes where catastrophic failures had already occurred, trees began to record progressively increasing ground instability 3–7 years before the events, as evidenced by a continuous, abrupt rise in ring eccentricity in individual specimens. The method was subsequently applied to the remaining two slopes to evaluate the likelihood of catastrophic reactivation in the near future. Our findings demonstrate that dendrochronological techniques, which offer long-term records of slope dynamics, can identify slopes at elevated risk of catastrophic landsliding well in advance. The applied methods show strong potential for forecasting catastrophic landslides and for assessing landslide hazards, slope stability, and the effectiveness of engineering measures designed to stabilise unstable slopes.The study was funded by the Polish National Agency of Academic Exchange NAWA, “Networking and education for innovative mitigation of geohazards in a changing climate” (BPI/PST/2024/1/00037 Strategic Partnership Program)

presentations.presentation_title: GO-EUREKA: GNSS-observation Based European System for Earthquake and Tsunami Hazard Assessment in Near-real-time
presentations.institution: Institut de physique du globe de Paris, Univesité Paris Cité
presentations.abstract: This contribution presents the GNSS-observation-based European system for earthquake and tsunami risk assessment (“GO-EUREKA”, https://iono-eureka.github.io), that is currently being developed through a cooperation of several research institutes from France, Italy, Norway, Brazil, Japan and Chile. GO-EUREKA will use quasi-continuous observations of ionospheric total electron content (TEC) from ground-based and ship-based GNSS-receivers, to assess earthquake and tsunami related hazards. Its final aim is to improve the existing tsunami early warning systems. The ionosphere is the ionized part of the atmosphere, located between ~60 to ~800 km of altitude. However, despite being high above the surface, it is sensitive to near-surface events. Thus, natural hazards (NH) generate acoustic/gravity waves that propagate upward and trigger atmospheric/ionospheric perturbations which can be further used for estimation of NH parameters. GO-EUREKA performs the following steps: 1) The data are collected and pre-processed by the module ALTRUIST (http://altruist-project.com), which provides in near-real-time the TEC data and the ground motion information; 2) Co-seismic and co-tsunamic ionospheric disturbances (CSID and CTID, respectively) are automatically detected in TEC data series by using algorithms recently developed by our group (e.g., Maletckii &Astafyeva, 2021, doi:10.1038/s41598-021-99906-5; Brissaud&Astafyeva, 2022, doi:10.1093/gji/ggac167; Ravanelli et al., 2024, doi:10.1029/2024RS008016; Fuso et al., 2024, doi:10.1007/s10291-024-01649-z); 3) Additional confirmation of the link between the detected disturbances and an NH event is done either by spatio-temporal analysis, or by a rapid simulation tools; 4) Inversion of NH parameters (under development) is done: 1) inversion of earthquake magnitude will be done from CSIDs detected in the vicinity of epicentral region, and/or 2) tsunami wave heights and velocity of propagation are estimated from CTIDs detected in the far field. These latter steps are currently under development. We will present our recent developments, and we will discuss future directions.

presentations.presentation_title: Hazard Potential of Pyroclastic Density Current–induced Tsunamis at Mt. Awu, Sangihe Islands
presentations.abstract: Volcanic tsunamis may be generated by dense Pyroclastic Density Currents (PDCs) that rapidly displace seawater. Historical eruptions of Mt. Awu (Sangihe Islands) produced tsunamis in 1856 and 1892, underscoring the need to assess future hazard potential. This study examines the generation and propagation of tsunamis induced by dense PDCs from Mt. Awu using the FLUIDITY and COMCOT numerical models. FLUIDITY simulations indicate that higher PDC density and lower viscosity significantly enhance tsunami wave amplitudes, following a characteristic sequence of rapid drawdown, maximum depression, and initial wave formation. COMCOT modelling of 16 scenarios shows maximum wave heights exceeding 8 m for a PDC density of 2,500 kg/m³ and a 2,000 m grid interval. The largest waves occur at near-source tide stations, particularly in shallow and open-water settings, while bay stations experience reduced amplitudes but delayed arrivals. Wave height and arrival time variations are controlled by shoaling, coastal morphology, and bathymetry. Dense PDCs from Mt. Awu can rapidly generate hazardous tsunamis, with bathymetric depth and coastal configuration exerting primary control on wave amplification. Continuous volcanic monitoring and effective early-warning systems are therefore essential for tsunami risk reduction in the Sangihe Islands.
